context-as-a-budget.explain:
## What it is

The **context window** is a hard cap on tokens the model can see in one call. System text, tool schemas, conversation history, retrieved passages, tool results, and the reply you want back all share that cap. Calling it a **budget** is the useful mental model: every token you spend on one consumer is a token you cannot spend on another, and every token has a price in money, latency, and attention.

A limit is a fence. A budget is an allocation. Teams that only respect the fence keep adding “just in case” text until a call fails or quality quietly drops. Teams that treat it as a budget assign shares, reserve output room, and can explain why a block is present.

The window is not a quality guarantee. Filling 90 percent of a 128k window is not automatically better than a 12k window that contains the right 12k tokens. Cost and prefill time grow with input size. Attention is finite: distractors that look relevant crowd out the sentence that actually decides the answer.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how products get expensive and worse at the same time. A support agent that appends every prior ticket, every tool dump, and a 20-page policy will eventually truncate the system rules, ignore the refund clause in the middle, or time out. Finance sees token burn; users see worse answers. The hidden cause is almost never “the model got worse”. It is an unmanaged budget.

Interviewers rarely say “tell me about context engineering”. They ask why a RAG demo died in production, why an agent loop costs 40 times a single call, or how you would pick 8k versus 128k. The senior answer names the consumers, reserves output, and says you measure quality against tokens per successful task, not against how full the window is.

## How it works + one small example

Before each call, add the tokens you already committed and the tokens you still need:

- reserved output (`max_tokens` or the provider equivalent)
- system and standing rules
- tool definitions
- durable plan or memory
- retrieved evidence
- recent turns
- older history (summary or drop)
- headroom for a tool result that might arrive this turn

An illustrative 64k call: 3k system + 4k tools + 20k history + 30k retrieval + 1k question = 58k input. If you also reserve 8k output you are already over. The failure looks like a mid-task cutoff or a silent front-truncate that deletes the rules.

A working split for the same window might be: 4k output reserved, 3k rules, 4k tools, 4k plan, 16k retrieval, 12k recent turns, 4k summary, 8k+ headroom. Elastic blocks (retrieval, history) shrink first. Fixed blocks (rules, current question) never get evicted.

Count with the **model’s tokenizer**, not characters. Log the breakdown on every request so you can see which bucket grew.

## Failure modes

1. **Bucket thinking.** “It fits, so ship it.” Quality often peaks well before the cap. You discover this only if you track accuracy and cost against context size.

2. **No output reservation.** Input is 90k of 100k and `max_tokens` is 16k. The provider rejects the call or cuts the answer. Reserve output first, then spend what remains.

3. **Blind front truncation.** The oldest messages disappear, which is often the system prompt or the user’s original goal. Truncate elastic blocks by policy, never by “delete from the left until it fits”.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Context is a budget shared by rules, tools, history, retrieval, and output. I allocate shares, reserve output, and justify every block by whether it changes the answer. More tokens are not better; the metric is quality per token, and I can show the per-block counts that prove it.
## A concrete walk-through

A support agent starts the week at 18k tokens per call and ends Friday at 70k. Nothing new was added to the system prompt. History and unfiltered search dumps grew. You draw the five consumers on a whiteboard, reserve 4k output, cap retrieval at 12k after rerank, and summarise turns older than eight. Monday’s p95 is back under 25k and the refund rule is still present on every failing trace.

## Interview follow-up

If they ask “why not just buy 1M context?”, say: that raises the fence, not the allocation. I still have to say who spends tokens and what I cut first. Then I give the Friday-to-Monday numbers.

## What I would measure

Tokens per successful ticket, share of calls over 80 percent of the window, and how often the system rule is missing from the rendered prompt.
keyPoints: All inputs and reserved output share one token cap.
Treat the window as an allocation, not a bucket to fill.
Reserve output and headroom before spending on history or retrieval.
Elastic blocks shrink first; rules and the current question stay.
Count with the model tokenizer and log tokens per block.
Quality often peaks well before the window is full.

questions.q: Why call the context window a budget instead of a size limit?
questions.a: Tokens are spent on competing consumers — rules, tools, history, retrieval, output — each with a cost in money, latency, and attention. A budget forces allocation and justification, not merely staying under a cap.

questions.q: A request fails only on long conversations near the limit. What do you check first?
questions.a: Input plus reserved max output versus the window, and which block grew (usually history or tool results). Fix that block’s cap and keep output reserved. Do not just raise the window.

questions.q: You have 100k of room. How would you spend it for a tool-using support agent?
questions.a: Reserve output, pin a small rules and tool-schema block, cap retrieval and recent history, summarise older turns, and leave headroom. Tune the split on evals, not by feel.

questions.q: Why can a 12k prompt beat a 90k prompt on the same task?
questions.a: Extra tokens add cost, latency, and distractors. If the deciding fact is already present, more text dilutes attention and can bury it. Measure accuracy against tokens per success.

questions.q: Finance asks why token spend doubled after you added a policy PDF to every call. What do you change?
questions.a: Stop stuffing the PDF. Retrieve the relevant clauses, give the policy a hard cap, and keep a short always-present summary. Show before/after block counts and task success.

context-rot-lost-in-the-middle.explain:
## What it is

**Context rot** is the observed drop in accuracy, instruction-following, and citation quality as a prompt gets longer, even when everything still fits. The model has the tokens; it uses them worse. **Lost-in-the-middle** is one shape of that drop: facts at the start and end of a long input are used more reliably than the same facts buried in the middle.

These are empirical effects, not a law of physics. Magnitude depends on the model, the task, and how similar the distractors are to the needle. A needle-in-a-haystack demo that finds a random UUID in page 47 can still fail a real task that needs two clauses from two documents and a constraint from the system prompt.

Rot is not the same as overflow. Overflow is a hard error or a truncate. Rot is a silent quality problem: the refund rule is in the prompt, the model just does not use it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Production RAG and agents die this way. Someone raises `top_k` from 5 to 40 “for recall”, latency and cost jump, and answer quality falls because the useful paragraph is now surrounded by lookalikes. Long agent traces do the same: the goal from turn 1 sits in the middle of 80 tool dumps.

In interviews, “we have a million-token window so we just dump the corpus” is a junior answer. The senior answer is: capacity is not quality; I measure position and length effects on my task; I shorten, rerank, and place the question and the constraints at the edges.

## How it works + one small example

Attention is spread across more tokens. Similar-looking passages compete. Instructions given once at the top can be overwritten by later “be helpful” text or by a retrieved page that contains its own instructions. Multi-hop questions are harder than single-needle recall because the model must bind several mid-context facts at once.

A concrete check: take a real prompt (system + 20 retrieved chunks + history + question). Place the one deciding sentence at index 0, in the middle, and at the end. Keep everything else fixed. Plot accuracy. If the middle placement loses, you have a position effect on this model and task.

Mitigations that actually move the number: cut `k` after a reranker; put the current question last; repeat the hard constraint near the end; process documents in map-reduce instead of one giant stuffed prompt; require a quoted span before the answer.

Do not copy someone else’s needle curve. Run the sweep on your traces.

## Failure modes

1. **More retrieval as a quality fix.** Raising `k` without a rerank and a cap adds distractors and pushes the useful span into the middle.

2. **Trusting a vendor needle demo.** Finding a planted UUID is easier than using a buried policy clause under conflicting text. Your eval set must look like production.

3. **Ignoring instruction conflict.** A long window that also contains “ignore previous instructions” in a scraped page is not only a position problem; it is an injection and labelling problem.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Long context is capacity, not quality. Accuracy can fall as the prompt grows, and mid-prompt facts are often used less than facts at the edges. I measure that on my own task, then shorten, rerank, and put the question and hard rules at the ends — I do not just buy a bigger window.
## A concrete walk-through

You plant the restocking-fee sentence at 10, 50, and 90 percent depth in last week’s real RAG prompt. Accuracy is 0.91 / 0.54 / 0.88. You cut k from 20 to 6 after a rerank and put the question last. The new middle score is 0.80 and cost per ticket drops. The curve, not a vendor slide, is what you take to the design review.

## Interview follow-up

They may say needle-in-a-haystack is solved. Reply: a UUID is easy; a conflicting policy clause under nineteen lookalikes is the job. I measure that.

## What I would measure

Recall by position, task success versus k, and citation rate of the intended chunk id.
keyPoints: Context rot is quality loss as prompts grow, even inside the limit.
Lost-in-the-middle: edges beat the middle on many models and tasks.
Needle-in-a-haystack is not the same as multi-hop production work.
Raising top-k without a rerank often makes answers worse.
Measure position and length on your traces, not a vendor demo.
Mitigate by shortening, reranking, edge placement, and map-reduce.

questions.q: What is lost-in-the-middle and how would you test for it?
questions.a: Models often use start and end facts more reliably than mid-prompt ones. Place the same needle at several positions and lengths in your real prompt and plot accuracy by position.

questions.q: RAG answers get worse when you raise top-k from 5 to 40. Why, and what do you do?
questions.a: Extra passages add distractors and bury the useful ones. Rerank, keep a small k, put the best at the edges, and evaluate k on a real set.

questions.q: A vendor slide shows 99 percent needle recall at 1M tokens. Why is that not enough?
questions.a: Planted unique strings are easier than using a buried, conflicting policy clause or binding two facts. You still need task evals, cost, and latency.

questions.q: The model ignores a constraint that is present on page 12 of 30 in the prompt. First debug step?
questions.a: Confirm the rendered prompt still contains the constraint, then run a position sweep. If middle placement fails, move or repeat the constraint at the edges and cut noise.

questions.q: Name two mitigations besides buying a larger window.
questions.a: Rerank and shorten the set; put the question and hard rules at the start and end; map-reduce over documents; require a quoted supporting span.

inspecting-what-actually-enters.explain:
## What it is

You cannot manage a context you never look at. **Inspecting** means seeing the exact final message list the provider receives after every template, middleware, memory injector, and framework default has run. That includes system text, tool schemas, retrieved chunks, injected “memory”, and any hidden developer messages.

The template is not the request. Frameworks duplicate system text, attach full JSON tool results, prepend traces, or drop a rule when a character budget is applied in the wrong place. Bugs that look like “the model ignored me” are often “the instruction was never in the rendered prompt” or “it was truncated”.

Inspection is a product feature, not a one-off debug trick. Every request should be able to produce a redacted trace: ordered blocks, token counts per block, which retrieved items were kept or dropped, and whether truncation fired.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On-call for an agent that “stopped following the refund policy” starts with the rendered prompt at the failing turn, not with a model upgrade. You will find a 40k search dump, a missing policy block, or a second system message that contradicts the first. That is a harness bug, and it is cheaper to fix than swapping models.

Interviewers like a concrete method. Say: I log the rendered request, I count tokens with the model tokenizer, I break counts down by section, and I never log secrets in the clear. Then I can answer “what did the model actually see?” in one query.

## How it works + one small example

Build a `ContextTrace` object on every call:

- `blocks[]`: name, role, source id, token count, hash, truncated flag
- totals: input, reserved output, window, remaining
- retrieval: ids included, ids dropped, scores
- redaction: API keys, emails, raw card numbers stripped before disk

A one-line log is enough to start: `sys=2100 tools=4800 hist=18120 retr=9200 out_rsv=4000 total_in=34220 window=128000`. When something fails, open the full ordered dump.

Example: a “be concise” rule lives in the prompt template, but a middleware wraps user text in another system message that says “be thorough and list every option”. The model follows the later instruction. Without a rendered dump you will argue about temperature.

Count tokens with the provider’s tokenizer or an equivalent library. Character length ÷ 4 is a planning guess, not an accounting number.

## Failure modes

1. **Inspecting the template.** The file on disk is not what went on the wire. Always dump after assembly.

2. **Unredacted logs.** Full prompts often contain customer text, tokens, and secrets. Redact, restrict access, and set a retention limit.

3. **No per-block counts.** A single “32k tokens” number does not tell you whether history or tools exploded. You will cut the wrong thing.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I treat the rendered prompt as the source of truth. Every call logs a redacted trace with token counts by block so I can see what the model saw and which bucket grew. Most “the model ignored the rule” bugs are missing, truncated, or contradicted text in that dump.
## A concrete walk-through

On-call: “the bot ignored the approval rule.” You open request abc123, not the template. The rule is absent; a middleware overwrote the system message after 32k characters. You fix the assembler, add a per-block count, and add a test that the approval sentence is in the rendered dump. The next similar ticket shows the rule at 1.8k of the system block.

## Interview follow-up

They ask what you log. Say: redacted ordered blocks, token counts, kept and dropped retrieval ids, truncation flags. Never raw cards or keys. I can pull one request id and answer what the model saw.

## What I would measure

Percent of traces with a complete dump, time-to-find a missing rule, and redaction-miss audits.
keyPoints: Log the final rendered request, not the template on disk.
Break token counts down by named block.
Use the model tokenizer, not character guesses.
Redact secrets and personal data before storing traces.
Record which retrieved items were kept or dropped.
Many ignored-instruction bugs are assembly bugs.

questions.q: What should a per-request context trace contain?
questions.a: The ordered messages and tool schemas as sent, token counts by block, included and dropped retrieval ids, and truncation events. Redact secrets and personal data.

questions.q: The agent ignores a system rule only after long sessions. How do you investigate?
questions.a: Open the rendered prompt at the failing turn. Check whether the rule was truncated, buried, or contradicted, and compare block counts to the last good turn.

questions.q: Why is inspecting the prompt template not enough?
questions.a: Middleware, memory injectors, and frameworks change the request after the template is applied. Only the post-assembly dump is what the model sees.

questions.q: You have a 32k token total and no idea why. What do you add this week?
questions.a: Named block counts (system, tools, history, retrieval, output reserve) on every call, plus a redacted full dump you can open for a single request id.

questions.q: A teammate wants to log raw prompts to a shared channel. What do you refuse and offer instead?
questions.a: Refuse unredacted customer text in a chat. Offer a restricted trace store with redaction, access control, and a short retention window.

allocating-the-budget.explain:
## What it is

**Allocating the budget** means giving each context consumer a named share and a rule for what happens when that share overflows. Without shares, the loudest producer wins: a verbose tool, a greedy retriever, or unbounded chat history.

A useful split names **fixed** versus **elastic** blocks. Fixed blocks are never evicted: standing rules, the current user request, a short plan, safety text. Elastic blocks have caps and a shrink policy: retrieval, older history, tool payloads.

The numbers are not universal. A 100k window for a coding agent and an 8k window for a classifier should not copy the same percentages. What transfers is the method: list consumers, reserve output, pin the fixed set, cap the rest, measure.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you stop a single search result from erasing the conversation. It is also how you explain a cost graph: “retrieval was uncapped, so every query stuffed 40 chunks”. Interviewers want a sketch with numbers, even if the numbers are labelled illustrative, and a sentence about how you would tune them with evals.

Saying “we use a big model so we do not need a split” is a tell. Saying “output is reserved, rules are pinned, history summarises after N turns, retrieval is top-k after rerank” sounds like you have shipped this.

## How it works + one small example

Write the budget as data, not comments:

```
output_reserve: 8_000
fixed:
  system_rules: 3_000
  tool_schemas: 6_000
  plan: 4_000
elastic:
  retrieval: 25_000   # rerank, then fill
  recent_turns: 20_000
  history_summary: 5_000
headroom: 10_000
```

When the sum of candidates exceeds a cap, apply the overflow rule for that block: summarise, drop lowest-scoring, or refuse the turn. Never steal from `output_reserve` or from pinned rules.

Example: a research agent’s web tool returns 40k tokens. The tool block’s cap is 4k, so the assembler stores the full page externally, keeps a 2k extract plus a handle, and leaves the rules intact. The next turn can fetch more if the extract is not enough.

Tune against a frozen eval set. If tightening retrieval from 25k to 12k does not move accuracy, keep the cheaper split.

## Failure modes

1. **No overflow rule.** Caps that are only comments get ignored under pressure. The assembler must enforce them.

2. **Evicting fixed blocks.** Front-truncation that deletes the system prompt to make room for another PDF.

3. **Copying someone else’s percentages.** A chat product and a batch classifier do not share a split. Re-derive from your traces.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I give every context consumer a cap and an overflow rule. Output and standing rules are reserved and pinned; retrieval and history are elastic and shrink first. I tune the split with evals and I can show the numbers for the last production incident.
## A concrete walk-through

You write the split as config: output 8k reserved, rules 3k, tools 6k, retrieval 20k, recent 16k, summary 4k, headroom 8k. A new web tool returns 40k. The assembler stores it and keeps a 3k extract because the tool cap is 4k. History still fits. Without the cap the rules would have been the thing that vanished.

## Interview follow-up

Ask them to assign percentages on the spot, then ask what overflows first. The answer that names fixed versus elastic blocks is the senior one.

## What I would measure

Per-block p95 versus its cap, overflow-action counts, and eval score after each cap change.
keyPoints: Name every consumer and give it a cap.
Fixed blocks are never evicted; elastic blocks shrink first.
Reserve output and headroom before filling evidence.
Overflow rules live in the assembler, not in comments.
Tune the split on evals, not by copying another product.
One uncapped tool output can starve every other block.

questions.q: How would you divide a context budget across components?
questions.a: Reserve output, pin rules and the current request, cap tool schemas, then give elastic caps to retrieval and history with a summary for old turns, leaving headroom. Justify with evals.

questions.q: One tool returns 40k tokens and crowds out history. What policy fixes it?
questions.a: Enforce a per-source cap: summarise or slice the tool output, store the full result externally, and let the model fetch more only if needed.

questions.q: What is the difference between a fixed block and an elastic block?
questions.a: Fixed blocks (rules, current question, short plan) are never evicted. Elastic blocks (retrieval, old history, tool payloads) have caps and shrink or summarise when over budget.

questions.q: After a release, answers miss the user’s original goal. The window is full of search hits. What leaked?
questions.a: The goal was treated as elastic and got evicted. Pin the goal and plan, and shrink retrieval first.

questions.q: Why should overflow policy live in code rather than in the prompt?
questions.a: The model cannot reliably refuse its own overflowing context. The assembler must truncate, summarise, or reject before the call is sent.

budget-inspection.explain:
## What it is

**Budget inspection** is the habit of logging **per-request token counts by section** so you can see which bucket is eating the window. It is the operational half of allocation: the split on the whiteboard is worthless if you cannot see yesterday’s real numbers.

A section is a named slice you control: `system`, `tools`, `history`, `retrieval`, `memory`, `tool_results`, `user`, `output_reserve`. The log is a compact record you can aggregate, not a novel. The full prompt dump is for a single incident; the section counts are for trends.

This is closer to request metrics than to prompt engineering folklore. Treat it like latency or error rate: every call emits it, dashboards chart it, alerts fire when one section steps out of its cap.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Incidents start with “the agent got dumb on Friday”. Inspection answers “retrieval jumped from 8k to 31k after we shipped a new connector” in one chart. Without section counts you will guess, upgrade the model, and miss the leak.

In interviews, walk through a table. Show that you know which section you would cut first and how you would prove it. That is more convincing than a lecture on attention.

## How it works + one small example

On the way out of the assembler, count each named block with the model tokenizer and attach the map to the trace:

```
req=abc123 model=... window=128000
sys=1840 tools=6120 hist=22110 retr=27400 mem=900
tool_res=1500 user=220 out_rsv=8000 total_in=60190
```

Ship these fields to the same place you send latency. Build a daily view: p50/p95 tokens by section, share of requests over 80 percent of the window, top request ids that overflowed.

Example: p95 `retr` goes from 9k to 28k the day you raise default `k` from 6 to 20. Task success is flat or down. You revert `k`, add a rerank, and the chart is the proof.

Keep the breakdown in traces you can join to a request id. A log line that is not searchable next to the user-visible failure is decoration.

## Failure modes

1. **Totals only.** “We sent 40k tokens” does not say whether to cut tools or history.

2. **Logging in one environment.** Staging uses short fixtures; production is where history and retrieval explode. Inspect production samples.

3. **No owner for a growing bucket.** If retrieval has no cap owner, the chart will rise forever.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I log tokens by section on every call and I can tell you which bucket ate the window last week. That number, not a vibe, decides whether we compact history, rerank retrieval, or shrink tool schemas.
## A concrete walk-through

You ship section counts on every request. Tuesday’s chart shows retrieval p95 jumping from 9k to 28k the hour a connector defaulted k=20. Success is flat. You revert k, add the chart to the weekly review, and give that connector an owner. The incident write-up is three lines of numbers, not a guess about the model.

## Interview follow-up

If they only quote a weekly total, ask which bucket moved. A candidate who cannot name sections is not operating the budget.

## What I would measure

p50/p95 tokens by section, percent of calls over 80 percent of the window, and alert time after a section step-change.
keyPoints: Emit per-request token counts for every named section.
Section maps belong next to latency, not only in debug dumps.
Totals hide which bucket leaked.
Alert when a section exceeds its cap or a p95 jumps.
Join counts to request ids so incidents are explainable.
Production samples matter more than staging fixtures.

questions.q: What is budget inspection in one sentence?
questions.a: Logging per-request token counts by named section so you can see which bucket is consuming the window and act on that bucket.

questions.q: Success is flat but spend doubled. The only number you have is total tokens. What is missing?
questions.a: A section breakdown. You cannot tell whether history, retrieval, or tools grew, so you cannot pick the right cut.

questions.q: Design the smallest useful budget dashboard.
questions.a: p50/p95 tokens by section, percent of calls over 80 percent of the window, and a link from an outlier request to its redacted trace.

questions.q: Where should the section counts be computed?
questions.a: In the assembler, after the final prompt is built, using the model tokenizer, then attached to the request trace.

questions.q: A new search connector ships and p95 retrieval tokens triple. What do you do first?
questions.a: Confirm the chart, cap or rerank that connector, and compare task success before changing models.

token-accounting.explain:
## What it is

**Token accounting** is splitting usage into the buckets that actually compete — typically **system**, **history**, **retrieval**, **tools** (schemas plus results), and **output** — then cutting the **largest low-value bucket first**. It is bookkeeping with a decision rule, not a pretty pie chart.

Accounting has two views. The **prompt view** is what you assembled (input sections + reserved output). The **bill view** is what the provider charged (input, output, cache write, cache read). You need both. A well-cached 20k prefix can be cheap on the bill and still rot the answer if you stuffed junk into the dynamic tail.

The cut rule matters. Shrinking a 400-token system prompt to save 80 tokens while a tool result is 22k is theatre. Always sort buckets by tokens × how optional they are.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the language of a good postmortem: “tools were 48 percent of input; we filtered the search payload and saved 60 percent of cost with no quality drop”. Interviewers will give you a table of counts and ask what you cut. Sort, justify, and mention the eval you would rerun.

If you cannot name the buckets, you will argue about temperature while the bill is a 30k HTML scrape.

## How it works + one small example

After each call, persist:

- prompt tokens by section
- reserved versus actual output tokens
- cache write / cache read if the API returns them
- dollars using the current price sheet (and a note that prices change)

Sort input sections descending. For each, ask: if I remove or compress this, does the eval move? Cut from the top until you hit a bucket that is both large and unused.

Example table (illustrative): system 2k, tools schemas 5k, history 8k, retrieval 7k, tool result 24k, output 1k. The first cut is the tool result: paginate, extract fields, store the rest. That single change beats a week of synonym-tuning the system prompt.

Use the provider tokenizer. Mixing models without recounting lies to you.

## Failure modes

1. **Cutting the visible prose first.** People edit the system prompt because they can read it, not because it is the hog.

2. **Ignoring output.** A runaway `max_tokens` of 16k on a task that needs 200 tokens wastes money and can hide a missing stop condition.

3. **Mixing tokenizers.** Estimating with a different encoding than production makes every cap wrong.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I split tokens into system, history, retrieval, tools, and output, and I cut the largest optional bucket first. I look at both the assembled prompt and the bill, including cache reads, and I recount whenever the model changes.
## A concrete walk-through

A postmortem table: system 1.6k, schemas 5k, history 9k, retrieval 8k, one HTML tool result 22k, output 400. You strip the HTML in the wrapper and the next day the 22k is 2k. Nobody had to debate adjectives in the system prompt. Finance sees the same table.

## Interview follow-up

Hand them that table and ask what they cut first. If they reach for the 1.6k system text, they are optimising what they can read, not the hog.

## What I would measure

Share of input by bucket, dollars per successful task, and how often the first cut is the largest optional bucket.
keyPoints: Split tokens into system, history, retrieval, tools, and output.
Cut the largest low-value bucket first, not the easiest prose.
Track the assembled prompt and the provider bill separately.
Include reserved versus actual output in the books.
Recount when the model or tokenizer changes.
Cache hits can make a large prefix cheap without making it good.

questions.q: Which bucket do you cut first, and why?
questions.a: The largest one that is optional for the answer — often a tool payload or over-retrieved chunks — because that is where tokens and distractors actually live.

questions.q: System is 1.5k and a tool dump is 20k. A teammate rewrites the system prompt to save 200 tokens. What do you say?
questions.a: Wrong first cut. Filter or offload the tool dump, then re-evaluate. System edits are for clarity, not for this saving.

questions.q: Why keep prompt-view and bill-view accounting?
questions.a: The prompt view shows what the model saw and where rot comes from. The bill view shows cache and price. A cached bloated prefix can look cheap and still be a quality problem.

questions.q: How do you include output in the account?
questions.a: Record reserved max output and actual output tokens. A huge reserve can cause overflow; a huge actual output can mean a missing stop or a rambling prompt.

questions.q: You switch models and every cap suddenly overflows. Likely cause?
questions.a: Different tokenizer and packing. Recount the same strings with the new encoding and reset caps from those numbers.

per-turn-budget-report.explain:
## What it is

A **per-turn budget report** is a **one-line breakdown after each model call**, stored on the **trace** for that turn, not only in a log pile. Agents make many calls per user request. A session-level total hides the turn where retrieval exploded or the tool schema list doubled.

The report is meant to be scanned in a trace UI next to the messages: turn index, section counts, remaining room, cache hit, stop reason. If the only place those numbers live is a text log with no request id, you will not use them during a debug.

This is how long-horizon agents stay honest. Compaction, offload, and stop policies need a number at the moment of the decision, not a weekly average.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

When an agent “got lost at step 17”, you open turn 17 and see `tool_res=31000 remaining=800`. That is the story. Without a per-turn line you will read 40 screens of tool JSON and guess.

Interviewers building coding or research agents will ask how you watch context over a loop. “We log totals” is weak. “Each turn writes a one-line budget onto the trace, and the loop consults it before the next call” is a harness answer.

## How it works + one small example

After `model.complete`, write:

`t=17 in=71400 rsv_out=4000 remain=12600 sys=2.1k tools=6.4k hist=18k retr=9k tres=31k cache_read=18000 action=compact_tools`

The loop reads `remain`. If it is below a threshold, run the overflow policy (compact tool results, summarise history, or stop) **before** the next call.

Keep the same line in the exported trace so a human and a later session can see why compaction fired. Do not rely on an engineer grepping hosts.

Example: turns 1–12 stay around 20k input. Turn 13’s web tool returns a docs site. The report shows `tres` jump. The policy replaces that payload with a digest plus a store id, and turn 14 is healthy. The line is the audit.

## Failure modes

1. **Logs only.** Lines that are not attached to the turn in the trace UI will not be used when it matters.

2. **Session totals.** A 400k session sum does not tell you which step to fix.

3. **No policy hook.** Reporting without a threshold that triggers compact/offload/stop is a dashboard, not a control.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Every agent turn writes a one-line token breakdown onto its trace. The loop reads remaining room and compacts or stops before the next call. I debug long runs from those lines, not from a weekly total.
## A concrete walk-through

Step 13 of a research agent jumps from 20k to 71k input. The one-liner on the trace says tres=31k remain=900 action=compact_tools. You open that turn, not the session total. The policy already replaced the page with a digest. Step 14 is healthy. Without the line you would have scrolled forty screens of HTML.

## Interview follow-up

Ask where the number lives. “In logs somewhere” is weaker than “on the turn in the trace UI, and the loop reads remaining room.”

## What I would measure

Turns with remain below threshold, actions taken (compact/offload/stop), and time to find the overflowing step in a 30-step run.
keyPoints: Emit a one-line section breakdown after every model call.
Attach the line to the turn’s trace, not only to host logs.
Session totals hide the step that blew the budget.
The loop should read remaining room before the next call.
Use the line as the audit for why compaction fired.
Cache-read tokens belong on the same line when the API sends them.

questions.a: Debug happens on a request’s turn list. A log line you cannot open next to the messages will not drive the next compact or stop decision.

questions.q: An agent fails at step 20. Totals look fine. What do you look at?
questions.a: The per-turn reports. Find the step where one section jumped and remaining room collapsed, then inspect that turn’s payload.

questions.q: What should the loop do with remaining tokens?
questions.a: If remaining is under a threshold, compact, offload, or stop before calling the model again, and record that action on the same report line.

questions.q: Write the fields you would include in the one-liner.
questions.a: Turn index, input total, reserved output, remaining, counts for system/tools/history/retrieval/tool results, cache read if any, and the action taken.

questions.q: Where does a per-turn report beat a daily dashboard?
questions.a: During a single long run, when you need to know which step overflowed and whether the overflow policy ran.

overflow-policy.explain:
## What it is

An **overflow policy** is a decided behaviour for the turn that will not fit: **refuse**, **compress**, or **drop the oldest elastic history** — and which of those you pick in which order. “It will probably fit” is not a policy. Neither is letting the provider return a 400 or silently crop the left side of the prompt.

Policy is part of the assembler and the agent loop. It must be deterministic enough to test: given a budget map and a candidate prompt, the same action fires. The model does not get a vote on whether its own context is dropped.

Refuse means fail closed with a clear error to the user or to the parent agent. Compress means summarise or slice elastic blocks down to their caps. Drop-oldest means evict the oldest **elastic** turns, never the pinned rules or the current request.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the difference between a controlled degradation and a random one. Unpolicy’d systems delete the system prompt, keep a 40k stack trace, and then “hallucinate”. Policy’d systems keep the goal, compress the stack trace, and stay on task — or they refuse a single huge paste instead of corrupting the session.

Interviewers will ask “what if the user pastes a book?” The answer is a policy, with user-visible behaviour, not “we have a 1M window”.

## How it works + one small example

A practical order:

1. If a single user upload exceeds a hard cap, **refuse** that upload (or take only a prefix) and say so.
2. Else **compress** elastic blocks in priority order: tool results, then retrieval, then old history.
3. Else **drop oldest elastic history** down to a minimum number of recent turns.
4. If still over: **refuse the turn** and ask for a smaller request or a new session with a handoff file.

Example: a user pastes 80k tokens of logs into an 32k effective budget. The policy refuses the raw paste, offers “store and summarise”, writes the file to object storage, and continues with a 2k digest. A different product might accept the first 12k with an explicit “truncated” warning. Both are policies. Silent crop is not.

Log the action on the per-turn report so you can see how often you refuse versus compress.

## Failure modes

1. **Silent left-truncate.** Deletes rules and the original goal. Looks like a model regression.

2. **Compressing the current question.** The one block you must keep verbatim.

3. **No user-visible signal.** The system answers from a chopped prompt and the user thinks they sent the whole file.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

When a turn will not fit I do not crop from the left. I refuse a single oversized paste, compress elastic blocks in a fixed order, then drop oldest history, and I tell the user or the parent agent what I did. The policy is in code and on the trace.
## A concrete walk-through

A user pastes an 80k log into a 32k working budget. The policy refuses the raw paste, stores the file, and continues with a 2k digest plus a handle. The user sees “I stored the log and used a summary; ask me to open a slice.” A previous version silently cropped from the left and deleted the system rules. That version “hallucinated.”

## Interview follow-up

“What if they paste a book?” is the question. Answer with refuse / compress / drop-oldest and what the user is told. Silent crop is not on the list.

## What I would measure

Refuse vs compress vs drop rates, user-visible overflow notices, and incidents where rules were truncated.
keyPoints: Decide refuse, compress, or drop-oldest before the call goes out.
Never silently left-truncate; that deletes rules and goals.
Compress elastic blocks first; keep the current request verbatim.
A single huge paste should fail closed or be stored, not stuffed.
Record the overflow action on the turn trace.
The model does not choose what to drop from its own prompt.

questions.q: Name three overflow actions and when you would use each.
questions.a: Refuse a single oversized input; compress elastic tool/retrieval/history when the working set is still useful; drop oldest elastic turns when you need room and recent work matters more.

questions.q: Why is silent front truncation a bad overflow policy?
questions.a: It usually removes the system rules or the original goal and keeps noisy recent dumps, so the model fails in a way that looks like a capability bug.

questions.q: A user pastes an 80k log into a small window. What should happen?
questions.a: Refuse or accept only a stored+summarised form, tell the user it was not fully inlined, and continue from a digest plus a handle.

questions.q: After overflow handling, the model no longer knows the user’s constraint. What went wrong?
questions.a: The constraint was in an elastic block that got compressed or dropped. Pin constraints and the current question outside the overflow competition.

questions.q: Where should overflow policy be implemented?
questions.a: In the assembler and loop, deterministically, with a logged action — not as a hope that the provider or the model will cope.

defending-a-window-size.explain:
## What it is

**Defending a window size** means being able to say **why this product uses 8k versus 32k versus 128k**, and **what you measured** to pick it. Window size is a product decision with a cost, latency, and quality curve. It is not “whatever the flagship model advertises this quarter”.

Smaller windows force selection and are cheaper and faster to prefill. Larger windows allow tasks that need a contiguous span (a whole contract, a long transcript) and reduce some retrieval misses. They also make rot, injection surface, and spend easier to ignore if you do not measure.

Defending the choice is a short argument: task shape, measured quality at two or three sizes, p95 latency and dollars per successful task, and the overflow story when a user exceeds it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Leadership will ask why the bill jumped after a model upgrade that “came with 1M context”. If you cannot show that the extra room improved a metric, you should not have turned it on for every call.

Interviews love this because it separates brochure knowledge from engineering. “We use 128k because the model has 128k” is weak. “Classifier stays at 8k; the contract-review path uses a long window only when retrieval cannot reconstruct the needed span; here is the eval” is strong.

## How it works + one small example

Pick two or three candidate sizes that your serving stack actually offers. For each, run the same eval set and the same traffic sample:

- task success / rubric score
- p50/p95 latency (prefill dominates on long input)
- tokens and dollars per successful task
- overflow rate and how often compaction fired

Example: an internal Q&A bot. At 8k with retrieval, success is 81 percent, p95 1.8s, $0.004/query. At 128k stuffing the top-40 chunks, success is 78 percent, p95 6s, $0.03/query. You defend 8k plus retrieval. A legal compare-two-full-filings path on the same stack might win at 128k because the needed span is the whole pair of documents.

Write the decision down: default window, exceptions, and the next review date. Re-run when the model or price sheet changes.

## Failure modes

1. **Defaulting to the maximum.** Every call pays for unused capacity and a larger attack surface.

2. **No measurement.** Opinions about “the model is better with more context” survive until the first eval.

3. **One size for every route.** A chat greeting and a repo-wide refactor do not share a window.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I pick a window from measurements: success, latency, and dollars per successful task, plus how we handle overflow. Small windows plus retrieval are the default; I use a long window only when the task needs a contiguous span that retrieval cannot rebuild. I can defend 8k versus 128k with those numbers.
## A concrete walk-through

You A/B 8k+retrieval versus 128k stuffing on the same 200-ticket set. Success 81 vs 78, p95 1.8s vs 6.1s, $0.004 vs $0.03. You keep 8k as default and open a 128k route only for “compare these two filings.” The decision is a dated note next to the eval.

## Interview follow-up

“Why not the max?” should get a table, not a brand preference. Offer a yes-case for the long window so you do not sound dogmatic.

## What I would measure

Success, p95, and dollars per success at each candidate size, plus overflow rate on the small window.
keyPoints: Window size is a measured product choice, not the brochure maximum.
Compare success, latency, and cost per successful task at two or three sizes.
Small windows force selection and are cheaper to prefill.
Long windows help when the needed span cannot be retrieved in pieces.
Different routes can use different sizes.
Re-measure when the model or the price sheet changes.

questions.q: What evidence would you bring to defend 8k versus 128k?
questions.a: The same eval and traffic sample at both sizes: success, p95 latency, cost per success, and overflow rate. Pick the size that wins on the product’s constraint.

questions.q: When is a much larger window actually worth paying for?
questions.a: When the task needs a contiguous span that retrieval would fragment, and an eval shows the long window beats a retrieve-or-summarise baseline on quality enough to justify cost and latency.

questions.q: A team switches every call to a 1M model ‘because we can’. What do you ask for?
questions.a: A before/after on success, latency, and cost per successful task, plus whether overflow and rot got worse. No metric, no switch.

questions.q: Why might an 8k classifier beat a 128k stuffed prompt?
questions.a: The deciding text is short. Extra tokens add prefill time, spend, and distractors without adding signal.

questions.q: How would you set window size for a product with both small talk and contract review?
questions.a: Two routes: a small default with retrieval for Q&A, and a long-context path only for documented global-span jobs, each with its own eval.

assembling-the-window-deliberately.explain:
## What it is

**Assembly** is the single code path that builds the final prompt from many sources. It is a function: given the task, state, and budget, return an ordered list of labelled blocks that already fit. It is not string concatenation scattered through handlers, middleware, and “just append this” feature flags.

A deliberate assembler has stages you can name: gather candidates, score and filter, fit to caps, order and label, emit and trace. If you cannot point to the function that performed those stages, you do not have assembly — you have leftovers.

The output should be reproducible. Same inputs, same prompt. That is what makes snapshot tests and evals possible. Hidden non-determinism (random example order, wall-clock timestamps in the prefix) is a bug.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Every feature team will try to inject “just one more paragraph”. Without an owner of the total, the window fills, caches break, and no one can explain the prompt. The assembler is that owner.

In interviews, describe assembly as an interface: features contribute **candidates** with a type, score, and size; they do not write to the wire. That sentence alone sounds like you have built a real system, not a notebook.

## How it works + one small example

```
candidates = rules + plan + memories + retrieved + turns + tool_results
chosen = fit(filter(score(candidates)), budget)
prompt = order_and_label(chosen)
trace = counts(prompt)
return prompt, trace
```

Example: billing support. The refund policy team registers a 400-token always-present clause. Search registers scored chunks. History registers recent turns. The assembler takes the clause in full, the top chunks until the retrieval cap, the last six turns, and emits labelled blocks. A new “tips” feature cannot sneak 2k tokens in except by registering a candidate that loses the fit step.

Snapshot-test the assembler with frozen candidates. When someone changes order or labels, the snapshot fails on purpose.

## Failure modes

1. **Feature append.** Three teams each `+=` onto a global string. Latency and contradictions follow.

2. **No test.** Prompts differ per code path and nobody reviews the rendered result.

3. **Assembly in the model.** Asking the model to “only use what’s relevant” from an unmanaged dump is not a substitute for a fit step.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I assemble context in one function: gather, filter, fit, order, log. Features submit candidates; they do not write the prompt. That is what makes the window testable and budget-aware.
## A concrete walk-through

Three feature teams each appended a paragraph. You replace the appends with candidate registration. Snapshot tests freeze a billing-ticket fixture. The next “tips” feature cannot land 2k tokens without losing the fit step. Latency stops climbing because the total has an owner.

## Interview follow-up

Draw the function signature: candidates in, labelled prompt plus trace out. If they cannot point to that function, they do not have assembly.

## What I would measure

Snapshot stability, tokens per feature, and how often a PR changes the assembled prompt on the frozen fixture.
keyPoints: Build the prompt in one testable assembler function.
Stages: gather, score, filter, fit, order, label, log.
Features contribute candidates; they do not append to the wire.
Same inputs should produce the same prompt.
Snapshot-test assembled prompts on frozen fixtures.
Own the total token count centrally.

questions.q: Why centralise prompt assembly in one function?
questions.a: It makes the final context reproducible, testable, and budget-aware, prevents duplicate or conflicting injections, and gives one place to trace what the model saw.

questions.q: Three features each append text and latency rose. How do you fix the design?
questions.a: Introduce an assembler that accepts candidate blocks, applies caps and priorities, dedupes, and emits an ordered prompt with a per-feature token trace.

questions.q: What are the stages of deliberate assembly?
questions.a: Gather candidates, score and filter, fit to the budget, order and label, then emit and log a trace.

questions.q: Snapshots of assembled prompts flap every run. What is likely non-deterministic?
questions.a: A timestamp, random example order, or unordered dict serialisation in the prefix. Make those stable or move them after the cache breakpoint.

questions.q: A teammate wants the model to ignore extra context instead of fitting. Why refuse?
questions.a: Models do not reliably ignore distractors, and you still pay for the tokens. Fit in code; do not outsource the budget to attention.

always-present-retrieved-or-excluded.explain:
## What it is

Every candidate piece of context is one of three classes: **always present**, **retrieved on demand**, or **excluded**. Always-present is the small, high-value set that applies to every call: role, safety, output shape, the current goal, the tool list for this task. Retrieved is large or situational: documents, old threads, code files. Excluded is a decision that this text does not change the answer — stale logs, resolved errors, decorative boilerplate.

The class is a property of the content, not a vibe. Ask three questions: how often is it needed, how large is it, and how costly is a miss. Small and almost always needed stays resident. Large or rare is retrieved. If a miss is catastrophic, keep a short always-present version and retrieve the rest.

Exclusion is not “we forgot”. It is written down. Otherwise yesterday’s debug dump becomes today’s default context.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This classification is how you stop a 15k policy manual from riding on every greeting, and how you stop a rare compliance limit from being a retrieval miss. Interviewers will hand you a pile (brand voice, 40 APIs, last 200 emails, a legal appendix) and ask what is resident. Sort with those three questions.

## How it works + one small example

Make the classes explicit in config:

- always: 800-token house rules, output schema, current ticket id, active tool menu
- retrieve: knowledge base, past tickets, CRM notes, via query + rerank
- exclude: marketing footer, raw HTML, resolved tool errors, duplicate chunks

Example: a refund ceiling of $50 is rare but a miss is expensive. Put one sentence in always-present (“refunds over $50 need approval”) and keep the full policy retrievable. The inverse: a 10k style guide used on 2 percent of calls should not be always-present; retrieve it when the intent is “write a letter”.

Revisit classes when traffic changes. Measure miss rate for retrieved rules and tokens wasted on unused always-present text.

## Failure modes

1. **Everything always-present.** The window is a junk drawer. Cost and rot follow.

2. **Critical rules only retrieved.** A retriever miss becomes a compliance incident.

3. **Accidental exclude.** A useful constraint lived in an old message that the assembler dropped with no record.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I sort context into always-present, retrieved, or excluded using frequency, size, and cost of a miss. Small universal rules stay resident; large situational text is fetched; exclusion is a decision I can show, not a side effect of truncation.
## A concrete walk-through

The 10k style guide was on every call, including password resets. You move it to retrieve-on-write-intent and leave a one-line voice hint resident. A $50 refund ceiling goes the other way: one always-present sentence, full chapter on retrieve. Misses on that ceiling drop to zero in the eval.

## Interview follow-up

Give them a pile (brand voice, 40 APIs, 200 emails, legal appendix) and ask them to sort. Frequency, size, cost of a miss is the rubric.

## What I would measure

Tokens spent on unused always-present text, retrieval miss rate on catastrophic rules, and excluded-but-leaked items in traces.
keyPoints: Three classes: always present, retrieved, excluded.
Classify by frequency, size, and cost of a miss.
Small universal rules stay resident.
Large or rare content is retrieved on demand.
Exclusion is written down, not an accident of truncation.
Promote a short form of a rare but catastrophic rule.

questions.q: How do you decide always-present versus retrieved?
questions.a: Weigh how often it is needed, how large it is, and the cost of a miss. Small and nearly always needed stays; large or occasional content is retrieved. Validate with evals.

questions.q: A rare compliance rule is only retrieved and sometimes missed. What do you change?
questions.a: Promote a one-line version to always-present and keep the long form retrievable, or add a retrieval trigger for those intents.

questions.q: Why is excluded a first-class class?
questions.a: If exclusion is implicit, stale dumps return through another path. Naming what must not enter the window keeps the assembler honest.

questions.q: A 10k style guide is prepended to every call, including ‘reset password’. Fix?
questions.a: Move it to retrieved, triggered by writing intents, and leave a one-line voice hint in always-present if needed.

questions.q: Give an example of promoting part of a document and retrieving the rest.
questions.a: A short refund ceiling in the system prompt, full policy chapters fetched when the user asks about refunds.

prioritising-what-matters.explain:
## What it is

When candidates exceed the budget you need a **priority rule**, not “whatever arrived first”. A workable order is: hard constraints and instructions, the current user request, the active plan or state, directly relevant evidence, recent turns, then older background.

Signals you can actually compute: reranker score, recency, source trust, whether the item was cited before, and a mandatory flag for compliance text. Combine them, then fill **greedily by value per token**, not by raw score. A 0.9 passage of 300 tokens beats a 0.85 dump of 4000 tokens if both cannot fit.

Mandatory items skip the competition. A legal disclaimer that must appear is not allowed to lose to a slightly higher cosine.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the answer to “how do you pick what goes in”. Interviewers want signals, a per-source cap so one corpus cannot dominate, and an eval that shows the priority function beats first-k.

Pure recency drops the original goal. Pure similarity returns near-duplicates. Saying those two failure modes out loud is most of the credit.

## How it works + one small example

Score each candidate: `value = relevance * trust * recency_factor`, then `value_per_token = value / tokens`. Sort, take mandatory first, then fill until the elastic cap, skipping near-duplicates (hash or embedding similarity).

Example: passage A is 0.9 at 300 tokens, B is 0.8 at 4000. You take A and a 400-token compressed B, not raw B. A third passage from the same blog as A is dropped by the per-source cap.

Protect the goal and the current question from this auction. They are not “evidence”.

## Failure modes

1. **First-k retrieval.** Rank is not priority-per-token and ignores length.

2. **No per-source cap.** One noisy site fills the window.

3. **Recency-only.** The opening constraint from turn 1 disappears.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I rank candidates by relevance per token, keep mandatory items, and cap each source. The goal and the current question are not in that auction. I evaluate the priority function; I do not ship first-k.
## A concrete walk-through

Ten chunks, room for four. You take mandatory disclaimer + three best value-per-token, with a per-source cap of two. Filename order is banned. A 4k low-score dump loses to a 300-token 0.9 passage. The original user goal is pinned and never enters the auction.

## Interview follow-up

Ask what happens under pure recency and under first-k. Naming those two failure modes is most of the credit.

## What I would measure

Eval of the priority function versus first-k, per-source occupancy, and goal-present rate after long threads.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What signals would you use to prioritise context items? Relevance (reranker), recency, source trust, past usefulness, and mandatory flags, normalised by token cost, then fill greedily. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is Pure recency keeps losing the user’s original goal. Fix? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `prioritising-what-matters`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Order: constraints, request, state, evidence, recent, old. Fill by relevance per token, not raw score. Mandatory items skip the competition. Per-source caps stop one corpus from dominating. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `prioritising-what-matters`.

Fill by relevance per token, not raw score.
Mandatory items skip the competition.
Per-source caps stop one corpus from dominating.
Pure recency drops the original goal.
Evaluate the priority function on a frozen set.

questions.a: Relevance (reranker), recency, source trust, past usefulness, and mandatory flags, normalised by token cost, then fill greedily.

questions.q: Pure recency keeps losing the user’s original goal. Fix?
questions.a: Pin the goal and plan as protected items. Only elastic history competes on recency or is summarised.

questions.q: Passage A scores 0.9 at 300 tokens, B scores 0.88 at 4000. Room for one. Which and why?
questions.a: A, or A plus a compressed B. Value per token is the rule; raw score ignores cost and rot.

questions.q: Why add a per-source cap?
questions.a: Without it, one site or one tool can consume the entire evidence budget with near-duplicates.

questions.q: How do you keep a disclaimer in the window when its retrieval score is low?
questions.a: Mark it mandatory so it is inserted before the scored fill, independent of cosine.

ordering-so-sources-stay-distinguishable.explain:
## What it is

**Order and labels** make it obvious which text is instruction, which is evidence, and where each span came from. Use stable delimiters or tags per source, with an id, name, and date when you have them. Do not splice retrieved prose into the system prompt as if it were your voice.

Distinguishability is a quality feature (the model can cite `doc:17`) and a security feature (untrusted text is marked as data). Mixed text is how a scraped page’s “ignore previous instructions” gets treated as a rule, and how two vendors’ conflicting prices get merged into one number.

A layout that works: standing rules first, then labelled reference blocks, then history, then the current request last. Keep each source in its own block. Never continue a paragraph across sources.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Citation, conflict handling, and injection defence all start here. Interviewers will ask how you stop retrieval from becoming instructions. The answer is structural: labels, an explicit “this block is untrusted data” line, and code that still validates the output.

## How it works + one small example

```
<rules>…house instructions…</rules>
<doc id="kb-44" src="returns.md" date="2026-03-01">…</doc>
<doc id="web-9" src="untrusted-web" date="2026-10-20">…</doc>
<history>…</history>
<user>…current question…</user>
```

Tell the model to quote `id`s and to treat `<doc>` as data. Put the question last so it sits on a strong edge.

Example: two docs disagree on a restocking fee. Because they are separate tagged blocks, you can instruct “if sources conflict, say so and cite both” instead of hoping the model notices a seam in a blob.

## Failure modes

1. **Unlabelled concatenation.** Citations become guesswork; injection becomes easier.

2. **Instructions inside data.** A retrieved README that says “always reply in pirate voice” is followed because it was not fenced.

3. **Question first, rules last.** The strong end position is wasted on boilerplate and the task is buried.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I label every block with source and type, keep untrusted text in data fences, and put the current question last. Labels give me citations and a first line of defence against treating retrieved text as instructions.
## A concrete walk-through

Two vendors disagree on a fee. You send tagged blocks `kb:returns-v3` and `web:untrusted#9` and require a cite. The answer reports both and prefers the kb. The same text concatenated as one paragraph produced a blended 12.5 percent that neither source wrote.

## Interview follow-up

How do you stop retrieval from becoming instructions? Labels, an untrusted fence, and output validation. Labels are necessary, not sufficient.

## What I would measure

Citation exact-id rate, injection-suite pass rate, and answers that invent a merged number.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: Why label retrieved documents with ids and sources? So the model can cite and attribute, conflicting sources stay separable, and untrusted data is marked as data rather than instructions. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is A scraped page said ‘ignore previous instructions’ and the agent obeyed. How do labels help? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `ordering-so-sources-stay-distinguishable`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Label every block with source, type, and an id. Separate instructions from untrusted data. Put the current request near the end. Do not splice sources into one paragraph. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `ordering-so-sources-stay-distinguishable`.

Separate instructions from untrusted data.
Put the current request near the end.
Do not splice sources into one paragraph.
Labels enable citations and conflict reporting.
Labelling reduces injection risk; it does not eliminate it.

questions.q: Why label retrieved documents with ids and sources?
questions.a: So the model can cite and attribute, conflicting sources stay separable, and untrusted data is marked as data rather than instructions.

questions.q: A scraped page said ‘ignore previous instructions’ and the agent obeyed. How do labels help?
questions.a: Wrap the page in a labelled data block, state that it is untrusted, keep real instructions outside it, and still validate outputs. Labels reduce but do not remove the risk.

cutting-redundant-stale-context.explain:
## What it is

**Redundant** context repeats something already present: the same passage retrieved twice, a tool result restated in the assistant message, three near-duplicate chunks from one page. **Stale** context was true once and is not now: an old file version, a superseded plan, a resolved error, a price from last quarter.

Redundancy wastes tokens and dilutes attention. Staleness is worse: the model can act on the outdated copy. Cutting is a first-class assembler step — hash or embed to dedupe, key by entity id to keep the newest, expire by timestamp, drop failed attempts once the lesson is recorded.

Cuts need evals. Aggressive similarity dedupe can drop two clauses that look alike and are not. Expiring too early forces refetch.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the everyday reason agents edit the wrong file or quote an old SLA. Interviewers will give you “v1 and v2 of the same spec are both in history” and wait. The answer is: key by path or id and keep one current copy, or store a pointer and re-read.

## How it works + one small example

Before fit:

- drop exact hash duplicates
- drop near-duplicates above a similarity threshold, keeping the higher-scoring or newer one
- for keyed entities (file path, ticket id, price list), keep only the latest
- drop tool payloads whose conclusion is already in the plan
- expire notes older than a policy, or marked superseded

Example: the agent read `app.py` at step 3, edited it at step 8, and both blobs sit in history. The assembler keys by path and replaces the step-3 copy with “see current file via read, last edit step 8”. Only one version can be acted on.

## Failure modes

1. **Dedupe by feel.** You drop a “similar” clause that changes the legal outcome.

2. **Keep both versions ‘for context’.** The model picks the wrong one.

3. **No expiry.** Memory notes from a previous project leak into this one.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I cut redundant and stale context on purpose: hash and similarity dedupe, one current version per entity, expire superseded notes. Stale is more dangerous than redundant because the model may act on it.
## A concrete walk-through

History holds app.py v1 and v2. The agent patches v1 and undoes the last edit. You key by path, drop v1, and keep “see current file, hash 9f2.” A later turn re-reads. Duplicate kb chunks are hashed out before fit. The stale-edit incident does not recur in the fixture.

## Interview follow-up

v1 and v2 of the same spec is the classic prompt. Key by id and keep one, or pointer plus re-read. “Models prefer later text” is not a control.

## What I would measure

Duplicate-span rate in assembled prompts, stale-file incidents, and eval after dedupe thresholds change.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: Why can stale context be worse than redundant context? Redundancy wastes tokens. Stale facts can make the model act on outdated state or contradict a newer instruction. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is An agent keeps editing a file from an old copy in history. What do you change? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `cutting-redundant-stale-context`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Redundant text wastes tokens; stale text can mislead. Dedupe by hash or high similarity before fitting. Keep one current version per entity id or path. Expire or replace notes that a later decision superseded. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `cutting-redundant-stale-context`.

questions.a: Key file contents by path, drop older copies, or store a reference and re-read so only one current version is in context.

questions.a: When its conclusion is already recorded in the plan or notes and the raw payload is stored externally if needed again.

questions.a: Raise the threshold, dedupe within a source only, or protect spans that contain distinct identifiers, then add those clauses to a regression set.

source-tags-on-every-block.explain:
## What it is

A **source tag** is a stable prefix on every injected span: who wrote it, which system, which id. Example: `[kb:returns-v3]`, `[user]`, `[tool:search#42]`, `[mem:ticket-881]`. The model can cite the tag. Your logs can grep it. The assembler can apply different trust rules per prefix.

Tags are not decoration. They are the join key between a sentence in the prompt, a row in the retrieval log, and a citation in the answer. If a block has no tag, you cannot say where it came from when the answer is wrong.

Keep the vocabulary short and stable. Do not invent a new prefix per request. Untrusted sources get an explicit untrusted tag, not a friendly display name that looks like your own docs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Citations, evals, and injection response all get easier. When a user says “where did you get that fee?”, you jump from the cited tag to the chunk. Interviewers will ask how you attribute. “We ask the model to be honest” is weak. “Every span is tagged and the judge checks the tag exists” is engineering.

## How it works + one small example

The assembler refuses to emit an untagged block. Each candidate carries `source_type`, `source_id`, `fetched_at`. Rendering is `[type:id]` on its own line, then the text.

Example answer: “The restocking fee is 15% `[kb:returns-v3]`; a forum post `[web:untrusted#9]` says otherwise, so I treated the knowledge base as source of truth.” Your eval can require that `kb:returns-v3` was actually in the prompt.

Use the same tags in traces. A missing tag in a log is a bug in assembly, not a style miss.

## Failure modes

1. **Pretty names only.** “From our help centre” cannot be joined to a chunk id.

2. **Trusted look for untrusted text.** A blog prefixed like an internal doc.

3. **Model-invented tags.** If you do not validate citations against the tag set in the prompt, the model will fabricate them.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Every injected span gets a stable source tag so the model and I can cite it. I validate citations against the tags that were actually in the prompt, and untrusted sources are tagged as untrusted.
## A concrete walk-through

The assembler refuses untagged blocks. A web result must render as `[web:untrusted#id]`. An eval item requires the cited tag to exist in the prompt. A model-invented `[kb:fees-9]` fails the judge and triggers a retry. Logs join the tag to the retrieval row in one click.

## Interview follow-up

Attribution without ids is folklore. Ask how they join an answer sentence to a chunk. If the join is a heading string, it will drift.

## What I would measure

Share of blocks with tags, citation-validation fail rate, and time to jump from a cite to a chunk.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What does a source tag buy you that a heading does not? A stable join key you can log, cite, and validate. Headings are prose; tags are identifiers. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is The model cites [kb:fees-9] but that id was not in the prompt. What do you add? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `source-tags-on-every-block`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Prefix every injected span with a stable source tag. Tags join the prompt, the retrieval log, and the citation. The assembler should refuse untagged blocks. Untrusted sources must look untrusted in the tag. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `source-tags-on-every-block`.

questions.a: With an explicit untrusted type, e.g. [web:untrusted#id], not a name that looks like an internal doc.

questions.q: Why refuse to emit untagged blocks?
questions.a: Untagged text cannot be attributed or trusted differently. Forcing a tag keeps assembly honest.

questions.a: type:id, optional timestamp, on its own line before the span. Examples: [kb:returns-v3], [tool:sql#18], [user].

assembly-order-tests.explain:
## What it is

An **assembly order test** checks that **swapping block order** does not make the model cite the wrong evidence or drop a constraint. Order is part of the prompt. If you never permute it, you will not know whether your layout is load-bearing or lucky.

These tests are not full product evals. They are cheaper fixtures: a known fact in doc A, a distractor in doc B, a constraint in rules. You assemble with the production order, then with A and B swapped, then with the question moved earlier. You record whether the answer still cites A and still obeys the constraint.

You are measuring two things: **position robustness** and **label usefulness**. If a swap breaks citations, your tags or your “question last” rule are doing real work and you should not “clean up” the layout casually.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Prompt PRs that “just reorder for readability” can tank quality or cache hit rate. A small order suite in CI is how you catch that. Interviewers like a concrete experiment more than a lecture on lost-in-the-middle.

## How it works + one small example

Fixture: rules contain “never invent a price”; doc A has “price is $12”; doc B has a forum guess “about $9”. Production order: rules, A, B, question. Variants: rules, B, A, question; A, B, rules, question; question first.

Pass if all variants either refuse or say $12 and cite A. Fail if any variant says $9 without flagging B as weaker. Run on the production model; order effects are model-specific.

Keep the suite small enough to run on every assembler change. Ten fixtures beat an unpublished notebook.

## Failure modes

1. **Testing only the happy order.** You will ship a layout you cannot change and do not understand.

2. **Confounding with different text.** The swap must keep the same tokens, only permute blocks.

3. **Ignoring cache.** A “better” order that puts a timestamp first may cost more than it wins.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I test assembly by swapping block order on fixtures with a known right source and a distractor. If a swap breaks citations or constraints, the layout is load-bearing and I do not reorder it for taste.
## A concrete walk-through

Fixture: rules forbid inventing prices; doc A is $12; doc B guesses $9. You permute A/B and the question. Production order and two swaps must still say $12 and cite A. A readability PR that moves the question into the middle fails CI and does not ship.

## Interview follow-up

Order is load-bearing. Ask them to describe one permutation test. “We thought about lost-in-the-middle” is not a test.

## What I would measure

Order-suite pass rate on assembler PRs, cache hit rate after allowed reorder, and citation accuracy by permutation.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What does an assembly order test change, and what must stay fixed? It changes only the order of labelled blocks. The text of each block and the question stay the same. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is A PR moves the user question above the documents ‘for clarity’ and citations slip. What do you do? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `assembly-order-tests`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Permute block order on fixtures and check citations still point at the right source. Keep tokens identical; only order changes. Measure both answer correctness and constraint obedience. Order tests catch ‘readability’ PRs that break quality or cache. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `assembly-order-tests`.
