recency-versus-reliability.explain:
## What it is

**Recency versus reliability** is a written rule for when a **newer message** beats a **more trusted document**. Chat is full of last-said-wins instincts. Knowledge bases are full of reviewed text. They conflict: the user says “we waived fees last week”; the policy says fees always apply.

You need an explicit precedence, not a hope that the model will “be reasonable”. A typical rule: user statements about **this** account’s exceptions win if they are in-session and you record them; standing policy wins for general claims; untrusted web never beats either; a newer **versioned** doc beats an older version of the same doc, not a random tweet from five minutes ago.

Write the rule where the assembler and the prompt can both see it. Apply it **before** the call when you can: drop or flag the weaker span instead of stuffing both and wishing.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is customer-support and RAG in one question. Interviewers will set up a conflict and watch whether you have a rule. “The model should figure it out” fails. “I tag trust levels and I have a precedence list; if they still conflict I make the model report both” passes.

## How it works + one small example

Trust tiers: `user_session` > `kb_current` > `kb_old` > `tool_raw` > `web_untrusted` for facts about **the product**. For **the user’s own data**, `user_session` and `crm` beat the kb. Recency only compares within a tier or within the same id.

Example: kb says restocking fee 15%. User: “Your agent already waived it for order 441”. Rule: treat as a claimed exception, do not overwrite the kb, check CRM or ask for the waiver id. If CRM confirms, the exception is now a stored fact with a timestamp; if not, say the policy still applies.

A newer kb version (v3 dated today) replaces v2 of the **same** article automatically in the assembler. A newer Reddit thread does not.

## Failure modes

1. **Last token wins.** The latest user sentence overwrites policy with no check.

2. **Kb always wins.** You ignore a verified exception and rage-quit the user.

3. **Recency across tiers.** A fresh untrusted page beats a stable internal doc.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I write a precedence rule: recency wins only within the same source or version line; trust tiers do not get overwritten by a newer weaker source. When they still conflict, I flag both instead of stuffing them quietly.
## A concrete walk-through

User: “you already waived the fee on order 441.” Kb: fee always applies. The rule is: do not overwrite policy; check CRM; if confirmed, store a dated exception. A Reddit post from this morning never beats the kb. v3 of the same article does beat v2 automatically.

## Interview follow-up

Set up the waiver versus policy conflict. “The model will be reasonable” fails. A precedence list plus verify-or-flag passes.

## What I would measure

Wrong-source preference rate, verified-exception rate, and how often untrusted web outranked kb in traces (target: never).
keyPoints: Write a rule for when a newer message beats a trusted document.
Recency compares within a trust tier or the same document id.
User exceptions need verification, not silent policy overwrite.
A new version of the same doc replaces the old one automatically.
Untrusted web never outranks internal policy on product facts.
If conflict remains, flag both sources instead of merging.

questions.q: When should recency beat a trusted document?
questions.a: When it is a newer version of the same source, or a verified fact about this user’s case. Not when a newer weaker source contradicts standing policy.

questions.q: User says a fee was waived; the kb says it always applies. What does your rule do?
questions.a: Do not silently overwrite the kb. Check the system of record or ask for evidence, then store a dated exception or follow the policy.

questions.q: A fresh forum post contradicts yesterday’s internal doc. Which wins and why?
questions.a: The internal doc, unless you have a reason to trust the forum. Recency does not cross trust tiers.

questions.q: The assembler keeps both v2 and v3 of the same article and the model mixes them. Fix?
questions.a: Key by article id and keep only the newest version; treat v2 as stale, not as extra context.

questions.a: In assembler logic (drop or flag) and as a short always-present instruction so the model reports remaining conflicts.

conflict-resolution-before-the-call.explain:
## What it is

**Conflict resolution before the call** means you **drop or flag contradictory snippets in the assembler**, instead of stuffing both into the window and hoping the model arbitrates. Models will average, pick the nearest sentence, or invent a blend. That is a bad place to resolve a price, a permission, or a medical contraindication.

Detection can be cheap: same entity, different numbers; explicit “supersedes”; opposite yes/no on the same slot. You do not need a full NLI model to start. When unsure, **flag**: keep both, add a `CONFLICT` wrapper, and instruct the model to surface the disagreement rather than pick silently.

Dropping is for the clear case: v2 supersedes v1 of the same id; a corrected tool result replaces the failed one. Flagging is for genuine disagreement across sources.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you avoid confident wrong numbers. Interviewers will put two fees in the prompt and ask what the system does. “The model will notice” is the fail. “The assembler marks a conflict and the answer must report it or retrieve a tie-break” is the pass.

## How it works + one small example

Before fit, group spans by entity key (`fee:restock`, `port:service-x`). If two remaining spans disagree:

- same source id, different versions → keep newest, drop old
- different sources, different trust → keep higher trust, mention the other in a one-line flag if useful
- same trust → wrap both in `<conflict key="fee:restock">` and require the model to say they disagree

Example: search returns “SLA 99.9%” and “SLA 99.99%” from two equally trusted runbooks. You do not average to 99.945. You flag the conflict and, if the task is contractual, refuse to answer until a human or a canonical table resolves it.

Log conflicts. A rising rate means a dirty index, not a smarter model.

## Failure modes

1. **Stuff both.** The model invents a compromise number.

2. **Drop the newer correction.** You treated a fix as a duplicate.

3. **Silent drop of the weaker source** when the user needed to see the disagreement (two vendors, two quotes).

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I resolve contradictions before the call: drop superseded versions, flag equal-trust disagreements, and never stuff both prices hoping the model will average them fairly. Conflicts are logged; they are data-quality bugs.
## A concrete walk-through

Search returns SLA 99.9 and 99.99 from two equal runbooks. The assembler wraps both in a conflict tag. The model must report the disagreement. A previous build stuffed both and answered 99.945. That number exists in no document. You log the conflict as an index-quality bug.

## Interview follow-up

Two fees in the prompt: what does the system do? Drop superseded versions, flag equal-trust pairs, never average.

## What I would measure

Conflict-flag rate, invented-compromise answers, and time-to-clean a dirty pair in the index.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: Why resolve conflicts before the model call? Models blend, pick the nearest sentence, or invent a compromise. Prices, permissions, and safety facts need a deterministic drop-or-flag step. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is Two equally trusted docs disagree on an SLA. What should the assembler do? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `conflict-resolution-before-the-call`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Do not stuff contradictory snippets and hope the model arbitrates. Drop superseded versions of the same id automatically. Flag equal-trust disagreements and require them to be reported. Never average two conflicting numbers in the assembler or the model. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `conflict-resolution-before-the-call`.

summarizing-history-without-losing-goals.explain:
## What it is

**History summarisation** replaces older turns with a short digest so a conversation can continue inside the budget. The failure mode is a generic recap (“we discussed the project”) that drops the goal, the constraints, and the thing that already failed.

A good summary is structured, not literary. It must carry: the user’s goal and constraints, decisions and why, open questions, current state, key identifiers (ids, paths, amounts), and attempts that failed. Recent turns stay verbatim. Only older turns fold.

The original goal should also live **outside** the summary, in a pinned block the assembler never compacts. Summaries drift. Pinned goals do not.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Long support threads and coding agents die here. After three compactions the agent “helps” with a different ticket. Interviewers will ask how you compact a 40-turn debug session. Name the template and the pin. “We summarise with the same model” is not enough.

## How it works + one small example

Trigger when elastic history exceeds its cap. Keep the last N turns raw. Send older turns to a summariser with a fixed schema:

```
goal:
constraints:
decisions:
open:
state:
ids:
failed_attempts:
next:
```

Bad: “Worked on a bug.” Good: “Goal: fix 500 on /orders. Constraint: no downtime. Tried cache clear (no effect). Suspected null customer_id in migration 12. Next: guard + rerun test_orders_create.”

Pin `goal` and `constraints` in a block that is concatenated after the summary, not inside it. After each compaction, run a quality check against a gold list of must-keep strings.

Do not summarise a summary if you still have the source segment. Hierarchical storage exists so you can go back to the raw slice.

## Failure modes

1. **Literary summaries.** Tone is preserved, ticket ids are not.

2. **Summary of summaries.** Drift after the fifth fold; the goal mutates.

3. **Compacting the last few turns.** You lose the exact error you are fixing right now.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I summarise old turns with a schema that keeps goals, constraints, decisions, ids, and failures, and I pin the original goal outside the digest. Recent turns stay verbatim. I test that known strings survive compaction.
## A concrete walk-through

A 40-turn debug thread is compacted. The digest keeps “fix 500 on /orders, no downtime, null customer_id, test_orders_create.” The goal is also pinned outside the digest. After three folds the pin still has the constraint. A literary recap that said “worked on an API bug” is rejected by the gold-list check.

## Interview follow-up

How do you compact a long debug session? Name the schema, the pin, and the check. “We summarise with the same model” is incomplete.

## What I would measure

Gold-list pass rate after compaction, constraint-present rate, and how often you refuse a digest.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What must a good conversation summary preserve? Goal and constraints, decisions with reasons, current state, open questions, key identifiers, and what already failed, so work can resume. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is After several compactions the agent forgets a user constraint. Fix? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `summarizing-history-without-losing-goals`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Use a structured summary template, not a prose recap. Preserve goals, constraints, decisions, ids, and failures. Keep recent turns verbatim; fold only older ones. Pin the original goal outside the summarised region. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `summarizing-history-without-losing-goals`.

compacting-large-tool-outputs.explain:
## What it is

Tool outputs — logs, HTML, query dumps, files — are often the largest context consumers and are mostly noise after they have been read. **Compaction** shrinks them immediately after use: extract the fields the current question needs, keep head and tail with a count, or replace the payload with a short result plus a handle to the stored original.

Compaction is not optional cleanup. If you leave a 20k log in the window, every later turn pays for it and the next error is harder to see.

Query-aware extraction beats a generic “summarise this”. The one line you need is “KeyError 'id' in test_a”, not a paragraph about CI in general. When the model must quote exact text, keep those lines verbatim and compact the rest.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the usual reason an agent loop gets expensive around step 10. Interviewers will give you a 30k log and a question about three failures. The answer is: extract in code, store the rest, return a digest with a pointer.

## How it works + one small example

Pipeline inside the tool wrapper, not in the prompt:

1. Persist the raw payload under `results/<id>`.
2. Deterministic reduce: row limit, field allowlist, strip HTML, head+tail.
3. Optional cheap summary aimed at the current goal.
4. Return `{id, n, digest, how_to_fetch_more}`.

Example: 15k test log becomes “3 failures: test_a KeyError 'id'; test_b; test_c; full at logs/run42.txt”. The agent can `read_range` if it needs stack frames.

Never compact away a value the next step must send unchanged (an id, a signature, a SQL error code) without putting it in a structured field.

## Failure modes

1. **Generic summary.** Drops the only failing line.

2. **No pointer.** You cannot get the rest back; the cut is irreversible.

3. **Compacting after ten turns.** The damage to the window is already done.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I compact tool output in the wrapper as soon as it returns: store full, extract for the current goal, keep a pointer. Exact ids stay in structured fields. I do not wait for the window to overflow.
## A concrete walk-through

A test log is 15k tokens. The wrapper stores it, returns three failing names plus `logs/run42.txt`, and never appends stdout. The agent opens a range when it needs frames. A generic “CI had issues” summary is banned because it dropped KeyError 'id'.

## Interview follow-up

30k log, question about three failures: extract in code, store the rest, pointer. Do not paste.

## What I would measure

Observation tokens per step, recoveries via handle, and incidents where an exact error string was paraphrased away.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: How would you handle a 20k-token tool output? Extract what the current goal needs or summarise with truncation markers, save the full output, and keep a reference so the agent can fetch more. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is Why is query-aware compaction better than generic summarising? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `compacting-large-tool-outputs`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Compact tool output immediately after it is used. Prefer deterministic extract and limits over a generic summary. Store the original and keep a fetch handle. Keep exact lines that must be quoted or replayed. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `compacting-large-tool-outputs`.

rolling-hierarchical-summaries.explain:
## What it is

A **rolling summary** updates one digest: when the verbatim window overflows, the oldest turns fold into a running paragraph. A **hierarchical summary** keeps layers: recent turns verbatim, medium-detail summaries per segment or session, and a short top-level digest. You can expand a layer on demand instead of living in one ever-lossier paragraph.

Rolling is simple and gets worse every fold. Hierarchy costs more calls and storage but preserves structure. The important rule: when you refresh a digest, summarise from the **source segment**, not from the previous digest, or drift compounds.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Long-horizon agents and multi-hour support work need this vocabulary. Interviewers will ask how you avoid “the goal mutated after ten compactions”. The answer is hierarchy plus a facts list plus summarise-from-source.

## How it works + one small example

Store:

- `raw/segment-k.json` — original turns for a slice
- `mid/segment-k.md` — 200-token structured summary of that slice
- `top.md` — 150-token session digest
- last 8–12 turns verbatim in the live window

When the live window is full, close a segment, write `mid` from `raw`, rebuild `top` from all `mid`s (or from `raw` if still cheap), and drop raw from the prompt — not from disk.

Example: a two-hour coding session becomes six mid summaries and a top that still says “goal: add 422 on missing SKU; tests in test_cart.py; next: handler”. A later session reads `top` then the relevant `mid`, not a tenth-generation blur.

## Failure modes

1. **Rolling only.** After enough folds the digest is fiction.

2. **Summarising summaries.** Same drift, fancier folder names.

3. **Deleting raw segments too early.** You cannot rebuild or audit.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I use hierarchy: verbatim recent turns, per-segment summaries, a short top digest, with raw stored so I can rebuild. I summarise from source, not from prior summaries, and I test that facts survive.
## A concrete walk-through

A two-hour coding session is stored as six mid summaries plus a 150-token top digest and raw segments on disk. When a fact goes missing you rebuild the mid from raw, not from the top. The tenth fold of a single rolling paragraph had already turned the goal into fiction; hierarchy stopped that.

## Interview follow-up

How do you avoid goal mutation after ten compactions? Hierarchy, facts list, summarise-from-source. Rolling-only is the trap.

## What I would measure

Fact-survival after N folds, rebuilds from raw versus from summaries, and disk retention of raw segments.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: Compare rolling and hierarchical summaries. Rolling keeps one digest, simple but increasingly lossy. Hierarchical keeps layers so you can drill into a segment, at the cost of more storage and calls. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is Facts disappear after the tenth compaction. What do you do? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `rolling-hierarchical-summaries`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Rolling folds old turns into one digest; it gets lossier each time. Hierarchy keeps layers you can expand on demand. Rebuild summaries from source segments, not from prior summaries. Keep raw segments until you are sure you will not need them. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `rolling-hierarchical-summaries`.

preserving-exact-structured-data.explain:
## What it is

Some strings must survive compression **verbatim**: identifiers, amounts, code, paths, error messages, schemas, dates, legal wording, API parameters. A summariser that turns “order 48213” into “an order” breaks the next tool call.

The method is mechanical. Extract those values into a structured side object **before** or **during** summarisation, carry the object unchanged, and **assert** after compaction that every tracked value still appears. Do not ask the model to “remember the numbers”.

Prose summaries are for gist: what we are doing and why. Data lives in JSON, a table, or a pinned facts list.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is why agents edit the wrong file or refund the wrong order after a “helpful” summary. Interviewers will ask what you never paraphrase. List types, then describe the assert.

## How it works + one small example

Maintain `facts.json`:

```
{"ticket":"INC-4401","branch":"fix/login","failing_test":"test_auth_refresh","amount_cents":1299}
```

The summariser is told to copy identifiers exactly and not to invent new ones. After the call, a script checks each value is in the final context (facts block or summary text). If a value is missing, refuse the compaction and retry or keep the raw turns.

Example failure: “about thirteen dollars” replaces 1299 cents. The assert catches it because `1299` is gone.

For code, keep the exact snippet or a file path plus hash, not a paraphrase of the function.

## Failure modes

1. **Trusting the summariser.** It will round, rename, and drop.

2. **No assert.** You find out when the wrong path is edited.

3. **Putting data only in prose.** There is nothing to check against.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I pull ids, amounts, and paths into a structured facts object, carry it unchanged, and I fail compaction if any tracked value disappears. Summaries are allowed to be lossy on gist, never on data.
## A concrete walk-through

facts.json holds ticket INC-4401, path cart.py, amount 1299. After compaction a script asserts those strings are still in the pinned block. A digest that said “about thirteen dollars” fails the assert and is not sent. The next tool call still uses 1299 cents.

## Interview follow-up

What do you never paraphrase? Ids, amounts, paths, errors, legal text. Then describe the assert, not a hope.

## What I would measure

Assert fail rate, wrong-path edits after compact, and must-keep field coverage.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: Why keep identifiers and numbers outside prose summaries? LLM summaries paraphrase and round. A structured object carried unchanged is what later steps can trust. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is After compaction the agent edits the wrong file path. How do you prevent this? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `preserving-exact-structured-data`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Extract identifiers, amounts, and paths into structured fields. Copy those fields verbatim; do not let prose own them. Assert after compaction that every tracked value is still present. Refuse compaction when the assert fails. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `preserving-exact-structured-data`.

reduction-vs-information-loss.explain:
## What it is

Every compression step trades **tokens saved** against **information lost**. There is no free reduction. The only question is whether the lost part would have changed the next decision.

Classify content before you cut: needed verbatim, needed as gist, needed as a pointer, not needed. Apply the cheapest safe method per class: keep, summarise, pointer, drop. Prefer **reversible** reduction (offload and keep a handle) over irreversible delete.

Judge the trade with task evals, not with a token trophy. A 70 percent cut that drops success is a bad trade. A 30 percent cut that leaves success flat is a good one.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Teams celebrate token dashboards and ship quieter failures. Interviewers will ask how aggressively you compress. The answer is a classification, a preference for reversible cuts, and a pair of numbers: success and cost per success, with and without the cut.

## How it works + one small example

For each block, tag a class and a method:

- approval text, prices, ids → keep verbatim
- old discussion → gist in the structured summary
- full log → pointer to store
- duplicate chunk → drop

Run the same tasks on a “fat” context and a “reduced” context. Keep the reduction only if success stays within a decided band and cost or latency improves.

Example: compacting search snippets from 12k to 3k leaves answer accuracy unchanged on 80 tickets; you keep it. Compacting the order-id list into “several orders” drops exact-id tasks from 95 to 60; you revert that class to verbatim.

## Failure modes

1. **Optimising tokens alone.** Success was not on the dashboard.

2. **Irreversible delete under uncertainty.** You guessed the future question wrong.

3. **One policy for all classes.** You summarise an approval the same way you summarise chit-chat.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Compression always spends information. I classify what must stay exact, what can be gist, and what can be a pointer, I prefer reversible offload, and I keep a cut only when evals say success held.
## A concrete walk-through

You classify blocks: approvals verbatim, old brainstorm gist, logs as pointers, duplicate chunks drop. A 70 percent token cut that dropped exact-id tasks from 95 to 60 is reverted for that class. A 30 percent cut on search snippets that left success flat stays. The trophy is cost per success, not tokens alone.

## Interview follow-up

How aggressively do you compress? Classification, reversible first, pair of metrics. Token-only dashboards are how quiet failures ship.

## What I would measure

Success and cost per success with versus without each cut, by content class.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: How do you decide how aggressively to compress? Classify how the content will be needed, use reversible methods when future need is unclear, and compare task success and cost with and without the cut. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is A team celebrates a 70 percent token cut but task success fell. What went wrong? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `reduction-vs-information-loss`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Every cut trades tokens for information; name the trade. Classify: verbatim, gist, pointer, or drop. Prefer reversible offload to irreversible delete. Measure success and cost with and without the cut. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `reduction-vs-information-loss`.

compaction-quality-checks.explain:
## What it is

A **compaction quality check** diffs the digest against a **gold list** of goals, ids, and open questions that must still be present. If the list is not a subset of the compacted context, the compaction is rejected. This is a unit test for memory, not a vibe read of the summary.

The gold list can be written by a human for fixtures, or extracted by code from the pre-compaction window (regex for ids, a pinned goal field, an `open_questions` list). The checker is deterministic. A second model “does this look complete?” is an extra signal, not the gate.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Without a check, compaction is an untested rewrite of state. That is how goals drift. Interviewers want a gate: “we fail the compact step if INC-4401 or the original constraint is gone”.

## How it works + one small example

Before compact, build `must_keep = {goal_text, *ids, *open_q, *amounts}`. After compact, for each item, require a string find (or structured field equality) in `pinned + summary + recent`. On miss: keep the raw slice, retry once with a stricter prompt, or skip compaction.

Fixture example: gold = `["fix 500 on /orders", "customer_id", "test_orders_create", "no downtime"]`. A digest that says “fix the API later” fails. CI runs five of these transcripts on every summariser prompt change.

Do not let the summariser write the gold list after the fact. That grades its own homework.

## Failure modes

1. **No gold list.** You only notice loss in production.

2. **Self-graded summaries.** The same model certifies its own completeness.

3. **Soft matching only.** “Orders endpoint” is accepted for a specific failing test name you still need.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I treat compaction like a rewrite of state and I gate it: a gold list of goals, ids, and open questions must still be findable after the fold, or I reject the digest.
## A concrete walk-through

CI holds five transcripts. Gold lists include the goal, an id, and an open question. A summariser prompt change that drops test_orders_create fails the job. In production a miss keeps the raw slice and logs the item for mining. The summariser does not write its own gold list.

## Interview follow-up

How do you know a summary is complete? External gold list, deterministic find, refuse on miss. Self-grade is not a gate.

## What I would measure

CI fail rate on summariser PRs, production refuse rate, and leaked-loss incidents that escaped the list.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What is a compaction quality check? A deterministic test that every gold goal, id, and open question is still present in the post-compact context, or the compact is rejected. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is Why not ask the summariser whether it kept everything important? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `compaction-quality-checks`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Diff compacted history against a gold list of goals, ids, and open questions. The checker is deterministic string or field equality. Reject the digest when a must-keep item is missing. Do not let the summariser author its own gold list after the fact. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `compaction-quality-checks`.

loss-budget-for-summaries.explain:
## What it is

A **loss budget** is a cap on how much named detail a summary may drop before you **refuse to compact**. It turns “don’t lose important stuff” into a number: at most N missing named entities, at most M missing numbers, zero missing items from the must-keep set.

Must-keep is still binary (goal, legal constraint, current amount). The loss budget is for the grey zone: extra entity names in a long story. If the summariser drops more than the budget, you keep more raw text or split the segment smaller.

This is how you stop a well-meaning aggressive compressor from silently deleting half the cast of a ticket.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

It is a concrete answer to “how do you know the summary is good enough?”. Interviewers hear a lot of “we prompt it carefully”. A budget plus a refuse path sounds like a control system.

## How it works + one small example

Extract entity and number sets before and after (`before - after`). If must-keep ∩ missing is non-empty: refuse. Else if `|missing entities| > 3` or `|missing numbers| > 1`: refuse or re-run with a larger token allowance for the digest.

Example: before has 8 person/org names and 4 amounts. After has 7 names and 4 amounts. Loss is one optional name — within budget. After has 8 names and 2 amounts — over budget, refuse, because amounts are in the tighter cap.

Tune the integers on fixtures. Support tickets might allow more dropped names than a finance reconciliation.

## Failure modes

1. **Budget of ‘whatever’.** You always accept.

2. **Budget so tight you never compact.** The window overflows instead.

3. **Treating must-keep as budgeted.** The goal is not something you are allowed to lose three times out of ten.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I give summaries a loss budget: must-keep items cannot disappear, and only a small number of extra names or figures may drop. Over budget means I refuse the compact and keep more raw text.
## A concrete walk-through

Must-keep is binary. Grey-zone names may drop at most three; amounts at most zero extra. A digest that loses one optional name passes; one that loses an amount is refused and the segment is split smaller. Support tickets get a looser name cap than reconciliation jobs. The integers live next to the fixtures that justified them.

## Interview follow-up

Turn “don’t lose important stuff” into a number plus a refuse path. That sounds like a control system, not a vibe.

## What I would measure

Refuse rate versus budget, must-keep misses (target zero), and how often you split segments instead of forcing a tiny digest.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What is a loss budget for summaries? A numeric cap on dropped named entities and numbers, plus a hard refuse if any must-keep item is missing. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is The summariser dropped one optional name and one amount. Your amount cap is zero extra losses. What happens? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `loss-budget-for-summaries`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: A loss budget caps how many extra entities or numbers a summary may drop. Must-keep items are binary: missing means refuse. Over budget: refuse compact or enlarge the digest. Tune the integers on fixtures for that product. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `loss-budget-for-summaries`.

two-tier-notes.explain:
## What it is

**Two-tier notes** means a **short rolling summary for the model** and a **longer external note you can rehydrate**. The live window gets 150–400 tokens of structured state. Disk (or a memory store) gets the page the human would want to read tomorrow: links, quotes, rejected options, full error text.

The short tier is what the model sees every turn. The long tier is what a later turn, a sub-agent, or a human fetches by id. Compaction updates both: shrink the short tier, append to the long tier, never the other way around.

This is reversible reduction applied to notes. The model is not the archive.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

## What it is

Some turns must stay **verbatim**: approvals, prices, identifiers, legal acceptances, permission grants, exact error lines you are about to fix. **When not to summarise** is a deny list the assembler honours even when the budget is tight. You may offload the surrounding chatter; you may not paraphrase “approved $1,200 on PO-88”.

Short + high-stakes is the test. A three-line approval is cheap to keep and expensive to get wrong. A 200-line brainstorm is the opposite.

If the window is still too small, store the verbatim turn as a fact field and a long-note quote, and keep those strings in the pinned block. That is storage, not summarisation.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the control that stops a compressor from turning a yes into a maybe. Interviewers will ask what you never send through the summariser. List the deny classes and say the assembler skips them.

## How it works + one small example

Tag turns as `verbatim` when they match: amount + currency, “approve/reject”, order or PO ids, credentials-adjacent values (which you should also redact), exact test names, quoted user constraints.

The summariser never receives those turns as input. They are copied into `facts` and into the live tail.

Example: user says “Cap the refund at $40, not $50”. That sentence is pinned. The rest of the 30-turn rant about shipping can fold. If a summary later says “user discussed refund limits”, the pin still has $40.

## Failure modes

1. **Summarising approvals.** You will mis-state the number.

2. **Budget panic.** The deny list is ignored “just this once”.

3. **Paraphrase in the long note only.** The live model never sees the exact cap.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I do not summarise short high-stakes turns — approvals, prices, ids, explicit constraints. They are pinned verbatim. I fold the chatter around them, not the decision itself.
## A concrete walk-through

The user says “Cap the refund at $40, not $50.” That turn is tagged verbatim and never enters the summariser. Surrounding rant folds. After three compactions the pin still has $40. A panic compact that paraphrased it to “user discussed limits” is a deny-list bug.

## Interview follow-up

What do you never send through the summariser? Approvals, prices, ids, explicit constraints. The assembler skips them even when the budget is tight.

## What I would measure

Verbatim-tag coverage on high-stakes turns, and any production case where an approval amount was paraphrased.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: Which turns should stay verbatim, and why? Approvals, prices, ids, and explicit user constraints — they are short, and a paraphrase changes the next action. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is The window is over budget and the last turn is ‘approved $1200 on PO-88’. What do you compact? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `when-not-to-summarize`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Do not summarise approvals, prices, ids, or explicit constraints. Short plus high-stakes stays verbatim even when the budget is tight. The assembler enforces a deny list; the summariser never sees those turns. Offload surrounding chatter; pin the exact decision strings. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. scratchpads-files-external-stores.explain:
## What it is

An agent should not hold everything in the prompt. It can **write to external storage** and read back a slice: a scratchpad (notes file or tool-backed pad), the filesystem (plans, logs, intermediates), a database or key-value store, a vector index for searchable memory.

Storage is cheap and survives resets. Context is scarce and evaporates. The pattern is: write the bulky thing, keep an index or a one-line claim in the window, open the thing when the next step needs it.

This is not “memory” as a slogan. It is an API: `write`, `read`, `search`, with naming, retention, and access rules. Unbounded folders of stale notes are just a disk-shaped context problem.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Long research and coding agents only work when the window is a working set. Interviewers will ask where a 40-page source goes. “In the prompt” is the junior answer. “A note per source plus an index, open on demand” is the job answer.

## How it works + one small example

Give the model tools that look like a small filesystem or store. After reading a paper, it writes `notes/smith-2024.md` and adds one line to `INDEX.md`. The prompt contains the index, not the notes. When writing the related-work section, it opens two notes.

For structured state, prefer a table or JSON keyed by id over a growing markdown diary. Cleanup is a policy: delete or archive notes when the task ends; do not keep customer text forever.

Watch what you store. Untrusted web text that is later reinjected is still untrusted. Secrets do not belong in scratchpads.

## Failure modes

1. **Re-reading every note every turn.** You rebuilt the bloated window on disk.

2. **No index.** The agent forgets the note exists and re-derives.

3. **Sensitive dumps.** Tickets and keys land in a world-readable folder.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I offload bulky state to files or a store and keep only an index in context. Storage persists; the window is a working set. I retrieve a slice when needed, and I clean up and protect what I write.
## A concrete walk-through

A research agent writes one note per source and a 20-line INDEX.md. The prompt holds the index. When writing related work it opens two notes. A version that re-read all fifty notes each turn is retired. Secrets are denied at write time. Task-scoped folders delete on complete.

## Interview follow-up

Where does a 40-page source go? A note plus an index, open on demand. “In the prompt” is the junior answer.

## What I would measure

Notes loaded per turn (target: few), write-deny on secrets, and leftover task folders after complete.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `scratchpads-files-external-stores`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Offload bulky or long-lived text to files, DBs, or indexes. Keep an index or one-line claim in the window, not the payload. Storage survives resets; context does not. Name, retain, and protect stored notes on purpose. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. active-context-vs-stored-context.explain:
## What it is

**Active context** is what the model sees on this call. **Stored context** is everything else the system knows: files, memory rows, history in a database. The skill is moving information between them at the right time, like a working set in RAM versus disk.

Active context should be the working set for the current step. Stored context must be **discoverable**: an index, descriptions, keys. If the agent cannot find a stored fact, that fact does not exist for practical purposes.

Eviction from active context is only safe after the item is stored or confirmed unused. Paging in too much recreates rot. Paging in too little recreates amnesia.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This analogy is how you talk about agents without mysticism. Interviewers will ask why the agent re-derived a fact it “already knew”. Missing discoverability or a missing “check memory first” instruction is the usual reason.

## How it works + one small example

At the start of a turn: decide the working set (goal, plan slice, last observations, retrieved hits). Everything else stays behind a key. Tools (`search_memory`, `read_file`) are the page fault.

Example: yesterday’s schema decision is in `decisions/schema.md`. Active context has “schema: see decisions/schema.md (chosen: additive migration)”. The agent reads the file only when editing migrations.

Make the inventory visible: a 20-line index beats a silent vector store the model never queries.

## Failure modes

1. **Invisible store.** Great notes, never retrieved.

2. **RAM = disk.** You load the store into the prompt “to be safe”.

3. **Evict without store.** You freed space and deleted the only copy.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Active context is RAM, stored context is disk. I keep a working set in the window, I make the rest discoverable with an index, and I never evict a needed fact without writing it down.
## A concrete walk-through

Yesterday’s schema decision lives in decisions/schema.md. Active context says “schema: additive migration — see decisions/schema.md.” The agent reads the file only when editing migrations. A silent vector store nobody queries is replaced by that visible index and a “check memory first” line.

## Interview follow-up

Why did it re-derive a saved fact? Discoverability or a missing check-memory instruction. The RAM/disk analogy is the explanation.

## What I would measure

Re-derive rate, index-present rate on boot, and average files paged in per turn.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Active context is this call’s working set; stored context is everything else. Stored items must be discoverable via an index or search. Page in on demand; do not load the store each turn. Never evict from the window without storing what you will need. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. ## What it is

For long tasks, write the **plan and progress to durable storage**: a checklist with steps, status, decisions, and next action. The agent re-reads it at the start of each window and after compaction. Conversation history is not a plan; it will be summarised or buried.

The file should stay short and structured. Status values are a closed set (`todo`, `doing`, `done`, `blocked`). Update after each completed step, with evidence, not in a batch at the end. Two writers need a rule (single agent, or lock) so they do not clobber each other.

Done means verified. A checkbox without a test or a check is how you get fiction.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the spine of a long-horizon harness. Interviewers will ask how work survives a context reset. “The model remembers” fails. “PROGRESS.md plus git, re-read on boot” passes.

## How it works + one small example

`PROGRESS.md`:

```
goal: add 422 when SKU missing
[x] 1 failing test (test_cart_missing_sku) — green as fail
[ ] 2 handler (doing)
next: implement handler, rerun test
blocked: —
decisions: keep existing 400 for other validation
```

On crash or new session: read this file, `git status`, tests. Do not invent a new plan. Mark done only when the named check passed.

Keep the file from becoming a log. Logs go elsewhere. The progress file is the current truth.

## Failure modes

1. **Done without evidence.** The next session undoes or repeats work.

2. **Plan only in chat.** Compaction deletes it.

3. **A novel instead of a checklist.** Nobody (including the model) can scan it.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I persist plan and status in a short durable file the agent re-reads after every reset. Steps become done only with verification. History is not the source of truth.
## A concrete walk-through

PROGRESS.md lists goal, five steps, next action, and a decision. Session two reads it before planning. Step 2 becomes done only when test_cart_missing_sku is red-then-green as designed. A novel-length diary is rejected in review. Two writers are not allowed; one agent owns the file.

## Interview follow-up

How does work survive a reset? Progress file plus git, re-read on boot. “The model remembers” fails.

## What I would measure

Boot-without-replan rate, done-without-evidence incidents, and file size (keep it scannable).
## How you would debug it on Monday

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Write plan and status to a durable, structured file. Re-read it at the start of every window and after compaction. Update after each step; require evidence for done. Keep the file short; do not let it become a log. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. ## What it is

A **note-taking agent** writes down what it learned, decided, and plans next, **outside** the window, and looks those notes up later. Notes are short, dated, atomic, and sourced. Separate facts, decisions, and open questions. Trigger writes at milestones and **before** a context clear, not only when the model feels like journaling.

Useful notes are easy to search: one claim per note or per bullet, with a path or url. Useful notes are humble about volatility: a port number gets a timestamp and a “verify live” habit.

Over-noting is noise. Under-noting is amnesia. The design problem is the trigger and the schema, not “let the model write a diary”.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is structured memory you can inspect. Interviewers will ask how an agent remembers a repo layout after a reset. “It takes notes at milestones and reads the index on boot” is a complete answer.

## How it works + one small example

After exploring a repo, write:

```

```

Triggers: after a successful search, after a decision, before compaction, at session end. Retrieval: `search_notes("auth tests")` or a pinned index.

Do not note every tool dump. Note the **conclusion** and where the dump lives.

## Failure modes

1. **Novels.** Notes become a second bloated context.

2. **No trigger before reset.** The interesting part was only in RAM.

3. **Stale facts treated as live.** Port 8080 from last month.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The agent writes short, dated, sourced notes at milestones and before resets, split into facts, decisions, and open questions. It searches them later and verifies volatile facts before acting.
## A concrete walk-through

After a repo walk the agent writes a dated fact: auth in src/auth, JWT, make test. The trigger is milestone plus before-compact. It does not note every dump — only the conclusion and a pointer. A port note is marked volatile; the next session verifies live before using 8080.

## Interview follow-up

How does it remember layout after a reset? Milestone notes, index, verify volatile facts. A diary of dumps is noise.

## What I would measure

remembering-vs-freeing-space.explain:
## What it is

Memory design is a tension: **remember** enough to continue correctly, **free space** to stay inside budget and quality. Every item gets an explicit decision: keep in the window, store then free, or drop.

Keep: goal, constraints, decisions, current plan, current question. Store then free: detailed evidence, logs, drafts. Drop: dead ends already noted, duplicates. Triggers: token threshold, phase change, end of a subtask.

Safe order when freeing: clear old tool results first (cheap, recoverable), then summarise older history, last of all irreversible drop. Free only after store or a confirmed “unneeded”.

Re-fetch rate is a health signal. If the agent keeps calling the same read, you freed too hard.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the policy interviewers want when they say “how do you manage context over a long run?”. Name keep / store / drop and the order you free.

## How it works + one small example

At 80 percent of the window, the loop:

1. Replace tool payloads older than two turns with handles.
2. If still high, fold history beyond the last eight turns into the structured summary.
3. If still high, drop excluded classes (resolved errors already noted).
4. If still high, stop and hand off to a new session with the progress file.

Example: a search dump from step 4 is stored; step 12 only needs “no hit in kb, see search#4”. Keeping the dump would crowd the handler you are editing now.

## Failure modes

1. **Hoard.** Rot and cost.

2. **Free too early.** Repeat tool calls and lost decisions.

3. **Free the keep set.** Goal disappears; the agent improvises a new one.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Each item is keep, store-then-free, or drop. I free recoverable tool results first, then summarise history, and I watch re-fetch rate to know if I was too aggressive.
## A concrete walk-through

At 80 percent of the window the loop clears tool payloads older than two turns, then folds history beyond eight turns. The goal stays. Re-fetch rate is watched; a spike after over-eager wipes puts back “last N plus one-line conclusions.” Dead-end errors already noted are dropped last.

## Interview follow-up

Keep / store / drop and the order you free. Re-fetch rate is how you know you were too aggressive.

tool-result-stores.explain:
## What it is

A **tool-result store** writes large payloads to an **id-keyed** store and puts **only a pointer plus a short digest** in the window. The observation the model sees looks like `{id, n_rows, digest, schema}` rather than 8,000 rows of JSON.

The store is the system of record for that call. Anyone — this agent, a sub-agent, a later session, a human — can fetch by id. The window is an advertisement that the result exists.

Ids should be unguessable enough for your threat model and not interpolated from untrusted text without checks. Cleanup belongs to the job: TTL, task-scoped buckets, delete on complete.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the standard answer to “the database tool returned 5k rows”. Interviewers want the store + digest + slice tools, not “we upgraded the window”.

## How it works + one small example

`tool_exec` writes `store/tr_7f3c.json`, returns:

```
id=tr_7f3c rows=420 cols=id,status,total
digest: 18 failed; sample ids 91, 94, 101
use query_result(id, sql) or read_rows(id, offset, limit)
```

The model can aggregate in the store (count, filter) instead of reading rows into tokens. Code processes data; the model reads summaries.

## Failure modes

1. **Pointer without tools.** The model cannot inspect the store.

2. **Digest that hides the question.** You stored 420 rows and summarised the wrong field.

3. **Forever retention of customer rows.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Large tool results go to an id-keyed store. The window gets an id, a count, and a digest, plus tools to slice or query the store. I do not paste the payload back in.
## A concrete walk-through

SQL returns 420 rows. The wrapper writes store/tr_7f3c.json and returns id, count, and “18 failed; sample 91,94,101.” The model calls query_result for the count by status. Customer rows expire with the task. A black-hole store without slice tools is not shipped.

## Interview follow-up

5k rows to answer a count: store plus digest plus aggregate in code. Do not paste.

## What I would measure

Payload tokens in the window, store TTL violations, and queries executed in the store versus rows inlined.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What should a tool return when the raw payload is huge? A store id, a size or row count, a short digest, and a way to fetch or query more — not the full payload. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is Why process aggregations in the store rather than in the model? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `tool-result-stores`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Write large tool payloads to an id-keyed store. The window gets a pointer, a count, and a short digest. Provide slice or query tools against the stored result. Process big tables in code, not as tokens. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `tool-result-stores`.

retrieval-keys-for-offloaded-state.explain:
## What it is

Offloaded notes are useless if a later turn cannot find them. **Retrieval keys** are the index: **task**, **entity**, and **recency** (and often type: fact, decision, result). When you write a note you attach those keys. When you need it you query by them, not by hoping a vector hits.

Keys should match how the agent thinks: `task=INC-4401`, `entity=cart.py`, `type=decision`, `t=2026-10-23T12:00`. A blob titled “notes2” is not keyed.

Hybrid retrieval works well: exact key filters first, embeddings as a fallback for fuzzy “what did we say about auth?”.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is why memory features fail in demos that used one note. Interviewers will ask how session 7 finds a decision from session 2. Keys, not “the embedding model is good”.

## How it works + one small example

On write:

```
{id, task, entities[], type, created_at, text, source}
```

On read for “why did we choose additive migrations?”: filter `type=decision` and `entity=schema` and `task=current`, order by recency, take top 3, then optionally embed the rest.

Show the agent the key scheme in the tool description so it writes keys consistently. Validate required fields; reject unkeyed writes.

## Failure modes

1. **Write without keys.** The store is a junk drawer.

2. **Vector only.** You miss the exact decision sitting under a precise id.

3. **Keys that are essays.** They never match twice.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Every offloaded note is keyed by task, entity, type, and time. Later turns filter on those keys first and only then use search. Unkeyed writes are rejected.
## A concrete walk-through

Writes require task, entity, type, timestamp. “why additive migrations?” filters type=decision entity=schema task=current before any embedding. Unkeyed writes 400. Session 7 finds session 2’s decision because the task id stayed stable in the progress file.

## Interview follow-up

How does session 7 find a decision from session 2? Keys, not “the embedding model is good.”

## What I would measure

Unkeyed-write rate (target zero), key-filter hit rate, and missed-decision incidents.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: Which keys should an offloaded note carry? At least task, entity, type, and a timestamp, plus a stable id. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is Session 7 cannot find a schema decision from session 2. What do you inspect? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `retrieval-keys-for-offloaded-state`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Index offloaded notes by task, entity, type, and recency. Filter on keys first; use embeddings as a fallback. Reject writes that are missing required keys. Document the key scheme in the tool description. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `retrieval-keys-for-offloaded-state`.

stale-memory-eviction.explain:
## What it is

**Stale-memory eviction** expires or rewrites notes that a **later decision has superseded**. Memory that cannot change is how agents honour a cancelled plan or an old hostname. Eviction is a write, not a hope that recency in retrieval will save you.

Triggers: a decision note that replaces a previous one on the same entity; a fact marked `superseded_by`; a TTL for volatile classes (ports, prices, branch names); a failed verification against live state.

Do not only add. Adding “we no longer use v1” while leaving v1 as a live fact is how you get both in the top-k.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Stale memory is a quieter bug than a missing note. Interviewers will ask how you stop last week’s architecture choice from surviving a revert. Evict or rewrite the keyed row.

## How it works + one small example

Notes have `status=active|superseded` and `entity`. A new decision on `entity=auth-store` marks the previous active decision superseded. Retrieval defaults to `status=active`. The old row remains for audit.

Example: note says “cache is Redis”. You migrate to the platform cache. Write a new decision and evict the Redis fact. If you only append, the agent will “remember” Redis on the next boot.

For volatile facts, a TTL plus verify-before-use is safer than eternal memory.

## Failure modes

1. **Append-only memory.** Contradictions pile up.

2. **Hard delete with no audit.** You cannot explain why the agent changed its mind.

3. **Evicting the current goal** because a cleanup job is sloppy.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

When a later decision supersedes a note I mark the old row superseded and retrieve only active ones. I do not leave both facts live and hope ranking works.
## A concrete walk-through

You migrate off Redis. A new decision on entity=auth-store marks the old fact superseded. Retrieval defaults to active. The agent stops generating Redis config. Append-only memory had been returning both facts in top-k. Old rows remain for audit.

## Interview follow-up

How do you stop last week’s choice from surviving a revert? Evict or rewrite the keyed row. Recency-only ranking is not enough.

## What I would measure

Active-versus-superseded mix in top-k (superseded should be zero), and wrong-stack actions after a migration.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What is stale-memory eviction? Expiring or rewriting stored notes that a later decision or a newer fact has superseded, so retrieval does not return both as live. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is You migrated off Redis but the agent still configures Redis. Why? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `stale-memory-eviction`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Expire or rewrite notes that a later decision superseded. Retrieve active rows by default; keep old rows for audit. Append-only memory becomes a contradiction set. Give volatile facts a TTL and verify before use. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `stale-memory-eviction`.

pointer-not-payload-rule.explain:
## What it is

The **pointer-not-payload rule** is: **never paste a file back into context when a path plus a one-line claim will do**. If the agent needs the bytes, it reads them in that turn. If it only needs to remember that `cart.py` owns checkout and last failed at line 88, that sentence is the payload.

This rule fights the reflex to “keep the file in chat so we have it”. Chat copies go stale the next edit and cost tokens forever. The filesystem or store already has the file.

The one-line claim must be specific enough to know **whether** to re-read: path, hash or mtime if you have it, and the conclusion.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

It is a crisp policy you can enforce in the assembler: if a block looks like a full file and you already have a path, reject it. Interviewers remember the slogan and the failure (two versions of the same file).

## How it works + one small example

After `read cart.py`, the observation becomes:

`read cart.py (hash=9f2, 120 lines): checkout in handleSubmit; test gap on missing SKU`

not the 120 lines. A later edit tool works on the path. If the model needs a snippet, it reads a range.

The assembler can detect accidental pastes (huge fenced files in history) and replace them with the last known pointer.

## Failure modes

1. **Pointer with no claim.** The agent does not know why the file mattered.

2. **Paste ‘just this once’.** The copy goes stale at the next edit.

3. **Hash-less pointers after edits.** You re-read when you did not need to, or you skip when you should.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Path plus one-line claim, not the file, in the window. I re-read when the next step needs bytes. Pasted copies go stale and I treat them as a bug.
## A concrete walk-through

After read cart.py the observation is path, hash, “checkout in handleSubmit; test gap on missing SKU.” The 120 lines are not in chat. An accidental paste of app.py from step 3 is stripped by the assembler to the last pointer. The next edit uses the file, not a stale copy.

## Interview follow-up

State the rule and the failure: two versions of the same file. Path plus one-line claim, re-read when you need bytes.

## What I would measure

Full-file pastes remaining in history, stale-edit incidents, and average observation size after reads.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: State the pointer-not-payload rule. Never paste a file into context when a path plus a one-line claim is enough; read the file again when you need the bytes. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is Why is keeping the file in chat dangerous after an edit? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `pointer-not-payload-rule`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Prefer a path plus a one-line claim over pasting a file. Re-read the file when the step needs bytes. Pasted copies go stale on the next edit. The claim should say why the file matters and how to know it changed. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `pointer-not-payload-rule`.

why-big-windows-do-not-solve-it.explain:
## What it is

A million-token window raises the **ceiling**, not the quality, latency, or cost floor. Long context still costs prefill time and money on every call (unless cached). Accuracy can fall as distractors grow. Reasoning over many facts is harder than recalling one planted needle. Agents still overflow on long runs. More text is a larger injection surface.

Big windows are a tool for tasks that truly need a global span. They are not a substitute for selection, compaction, or a harness. “We dumped the wiki” is a strategy with a measured win condition, not a default.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the myth interviewers want you to puncture. The junior line is the brochure context length. The senior line is: capacity ≠ quality; I still retrieve, I still measure, I still cap.

On the job, turning on max context for every route is how bills jump and latency SLOs die without a quality win.

## How it works + one small example

Five reasons, with a check for each:

1. Cost/latency — compare p95 and $ at 8k vs 128k on the same task.
2. Rot — plot accuracy vs stuffed size.
3. Multi-fact hardness — evals that need two clauses, not one UUID.
4. Overflow — a 4-hour agent still exceeds any finite window.
5. Injection — more retrieved HTML is more untrusted instructions.

Example: answering “what is the refund window?” from a 500-page handbook. Stuffing the book sometimes works and is slow. Retrieving three policy pages is cheaper and often more accurate. Summarising the whole book is the wrong tool for a pointed question.

When the task is “write an executive summary of this entire filing”, a long window or map-reduce is justified. Say that exception out loud.

## Failure modes

1. **Default to max.** Every greeting pays for unused capacity.

2. **Needle demos as proof.** Unique strings are easy mode.

3. **Ignoring the agent loop.** The window is per call; the work is many calls.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Big windows add capacity, not quality or a free lunch. I still select, I still measure cost and accuracy, and I use a long window only when the task needs a span retrieval cannot rebuild.
## A concrete walk-through

A team enables 1M on every route. p95 triples, quality is flat, the wiki dump still misses a two-clause question. You revert the default to 8k+retrieval and keep a long route for full-filing summaries. The brochure length is no longer the product default.

## Interview follow-up

Puncture the myth: capacity is not quality. Give a yes-case for long context so you sound selective, not allergic.

## What I would measure

Quality, p95, and $ per success at max versus selected context, plus overflow rate on long-running agents.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: Why not use the largest context window for everything? Cost and latency grow with input, accuracy can degrade, and agents still overflow. Selecting relevant context is usually cheaper and more reliable. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is When is a very large window justified? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `why-big-windows-do-not-solve-it`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: A larger window is capacity, not a quality or cost fix. Prefill time and spend still grow with input size. Accuracy can fall as distractors and length grow. Needle recall is easier than multi-fact production tasks. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `why-big-windows-do-not-solve-it`.

managing-lost-in-the-middle.explain:
## What it is

Practical mitigations for position effects: put **key instructions and the question at the edges**; **shorten** with a reranker; **order by relevance** so the best items are not all buried; **map-reduce** documents instead of one stuffed prompt; **structure** with headings and ids; **require quoted evidence** before the answer.

The size of the effect is model- and task-specific. You manage it by measuring a position sweep, then applying the cheapest fix that moves the metric. Reordering without a check can create a new bias toward the first item.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the hands-on follow-up to “lost-in-the-middle exists”. Interviewers want two or three mitigations and a test, not a paper citation.

## How it works + one small example

Default layout: rules (start), evidence (best first and last, middling in the middle or dropped), question (end). After rerank, keep k=5 not k=40.

If a middle document is still required, do not stuff it among 30 others — process it in a map step and pass the extract forward.

Example: ten chunks, the answer lives in chunk 6. Accuracy is low. Rerank puts that chunk first or last, or you map each chunk to a yes/no + quote and reduce. Adding ten more chunks is the wrong experiment.

Ask the model to quote the supporting id before the answer so you can see whether it used the middle span.

## Failure modes

1. **More context as the fix.** You deepen the haystack.

2. **Copying another model’s layout.** Effects differ.

3. **Reordering that always prefers the first doc.** You created primacy bias.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I manage lost-in-the-middle by shortening, placing the question and rules at the edges, and map-reducing when a middle span must be used. I confirm with a position sweep on my model.
## A concrete walk-through

Ten chunks, answer in chunk 6, middle score poor. You rerank, keep five, put the winner next to the question, and require a quote of the id. Adding ten more chunks is rejected as an experiment. A first-item-only bias appears; you keep a conflict path so a second source can still surface.

## Interview follow-up

Name two mitigations and a test. Reordering without a sweep can create primacy bias — say that.

## What I would measure

Position curve after packing changes, citation of non-first sources, and k versus accuracy.
## How you would debug it on Monday

If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is Answers ignore the middle three of ten retrieved docs. What do you try? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `managing-lost-in-the-middle`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Put critical instructions and the question at the start and end. Rerank and shorten; do not deepen the haystack. Map-reduce when a document would otherwise sit in the middle. Require a quoted span or id before the answer. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped.
