what-not-to-cache.explain:
## What it is

**What not to cache**: **secrets**, **per-user personal data**, and **one-off tool results** do not belong in the stable prefix. Caching is reuse. Reuse of a secret increases blast radius. Reuse of PII across users is a privacy bug and also a cache-miss generator if you were hoping for a shared prefix. One-off tool dumps are not stable; putting them before the breakpoint guarantees misses and stores junk in a cache you do not control as tightly as your own store.

The stable prefix should be **the same for many requests** and **safe if retained** for the provider’s cache lifetime. If you would not put it in a shared CDN, do not put it in the cached prefix.

User-specific config can still be sent — **after** the breakpoint.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the safety companion to cache-hit engineering. Interviewers will ask what you refuse to put in the cached block. Name secrets, PII, and one-off results.

## How it works + one small example

Allowlist the prefix: house rules, non-secret tool schemas, public or company-wide reference text. Denylist: API keys (which should not be in prompts at all), account numbers, free-text user memory, raw tool dumps, session tokens.

Example: a “remember this customer is in Germany” note is state, not prefix. A GDPR-sensitive transcript is not a cached manual.

If a provider’s cache is billed and stored on their side, treat that as a third-party store in your threat model. Minimise.

## Failure modes

1. **Keys in the system prompt.** Wrong even without caching; worse with it.

2. **Per-user memory in the prefix.** Misses and a PII cache.

3. **Caching the last tool result** “because it might help the next user”.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I only cache content that is shared and non-sensitive. Secrets, per-user data, and one-off tool results stay out of the stable prefix and go after the breakpoint or into my own store.
## A concrete walk-through

A review finds an API key and a per-user “lives in Germany” note in the cached system prompt. You rotate the key, treat the cache as a leak surface, move the note after the breakpoint, and add a CI denylist. Last-search-dump-as-prefix is rejected: that is what your result store is for.

## Interview follow-up

What do you refuse to cache? Secrets, PII, one-off results. If it would be wrong on a CDN, it is wrong in the prefix.

## What I would measure

Denylist hits in CI, PII-before-breakpoint findings, and keys in prompts (target zero).
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What three classes should stay out of the stable cached prefix? Secrets, per-user personal data, and one-off tool results. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is Why is per-user memory a bad prefix even if it is not a secret? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `what-not-to-cache`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Do not put secrets in a cached prefix — or in the prompt at all. Per-user personal data belongs after the breakpoint. One-off tool results are not stable and should not be cached as prefix. The prefix should be safe to reuse across many requests. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. what-an-agent-harness-is.explain:
## What it is

The **agent harness** is everything around the model that turns it into an agent: the loop that calls it, the tools, context assembly, memory, permissions, sandbox, logging, retries, and stop conditions. The model proposes. The harness executes, constrains, and remembers.

Two systems with the same model can differ hugely because of the harness. It decides what the model sees each step, which actions are possible, and what happens on failure. It is mostly deterministic code you can test. The model is the stochastic part.

Name the pieces: prompt/context builder, tool registry and executor, state store, guardrails and approvals, observability, budget and termination. If you cannot point to those, you have a chat wrapper, not a harness.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the senior framing for agents. Interviewers who have shipped these ask about the harness first. “We use model X” is not a design. “Here is the loop, the caps, the progress file, and what code enforces” is.

On the job, reliability work is usually harness work: better context, better tools, better checks.

## How it works + one small example

```
while not done and within caps:
  ctx = assemble(state, budget)
  out = model(ctx, tools=menu)
  if out.tool: state += run(out.tool)  # validated, sandboxed
  else: done = True
```

Around that: progress file, observation caps, permission checks, a trace per turn.

Example: two coding agents, same model. One has tests-as-a-gate, a progress file, and a schema budget. The other pastes the repo and hopes. The first completes; the second loops. The model did not change.

## Failure modes

1. **Calling the chat API a harness.** No caps, no assembly, no enforcement.

2. **Blaming the model by default.** You skip the cheaper fixes.

3. **Harness logic in the prompt only.** The model can ignore it.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The harness is the loop, tools, context, memory, and guardrails around the model. I treat it as testable code. Same model, better harness, better agent.
## A concrete walk-through

Two coding agents, same model. Yours has assembly, a progress file, test gates, schema budgets, and traces. The other pastes the repo into chat. Yours finishes the 422 ticket; the other loops. The write-up does not mention the model name in the first paragraph. It names the harness pieces.

## Interview follow-up

Harness first, model second. If they cannot list loop, tools, context, memory, stop, they have a wrapper.

## What I would measure

Task success at fixed model across harness versions, and how often incidents close as harness versus model.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What is an agent harness? The software around the model: the loop, tool execution, context assembly, memory, permissions, logging, and stop logic that turns model outputs into controlled actions. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is Why can a weaker model with a better harness beat a stronger model with a poor one? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `what-an-agent-harness-is`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Harness = loop, tools, context assembly, memory, permissions, stop logic. The model proposes; the harness executes and constrains. Same model, different harness, different reliability. Most of the harness is deterministic code you can test. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. harness-problems-vs-model-problems.explain:
## What it is

When an agent fails, decide whether the **model** lacked capability or the **harness** set it up to fail. Harness problems: missing information in context, truncated instructions, confusing schemas, useless tool errors, no verification, no retry, state lost between windows. Model problems: wrong reasoning given complete, clear context and decent tools; inventing facts despite evidence; failing a skill even with a good setup.

The diagnostic: could a competent human have succeeded with **exactly this input and these tools**? If not, fix the harness. Only then try a stronger model. Blaming the model first hides cheap bugs and raises spend.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This fork is how you run an incident. Interviewers will give you a cryptic tool error loop and wait for “harness”. Upgrading the model is the trap answer.

## How it works + one small example

Read the trace. List: what the model saw, what it tried, what the tool returned, whether a stop cap hit.

Example: the needed file was never in context. Human would also fail. Harness: assembler or retrieval miss. Example: the file is there, the test command is documented, the model writes a different function. Maybe model, but first check whether the instruction was buried.

Another classic harness fail: tool returns `Error: 500` with no body. No human could recover either. Return a useful error and retry policy.

## Failure modes

1. **Default to a model upgrade.** The bug was a truncated rule.

2. **No traces.** You cannot run the human test.

3. **Calling every failure ‘hallucination’.** That word hides missing context.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I ask whether a competent human could succeed from this exact prompt and toolset. If not, it is a harness problem. I inspect traces before I change models.
## A concrete walk-through

Trace: needed file never attached. Human would fail too. You fix retrieval and do not bump the model. Next week a cryptic `Error: 500` loop is fixed with a useful tool error. A later case has the file, the command, and a still-wrong function — that one is a model experiment after the setup is fair.

## Interview follow-up

Cryptic tool-error loop: harness. Upgrading the model is the trap. Run the “would a human succeed?” test.

## What I would measure

Incident classification harness/model, time-to-trace, and upgrades reverted because the bug was missing context.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: How do you tell a harness failure from a model failure? Inspect the trace. If a competent human could not succeed from that input and those tools, it is a harness issue; otherwise it may be model capability. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is The agent repeatedly fails a tool call with a cryptic error. Harness or model? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `harness-problems-vs-model-problems`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Ask whether a human could succeed with this exact input and tools. Most early failures are harness failures. Missing context, bad schemas, and useless errors are harness issues. Inspect traces before you change models. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `harness-problems-vs-model-problems`.

designing-the-agent-loop.explain:
## What it is

The **agent loop**: assemble context, call the model, parse the output, execute any tool calls, append observations, check stop conditions, repeat.

Design choices you must make on purpose: termination (final answer, step cap, token or cost budget, wall clock); error handling (tool errors as observations, backoff, circuit breakers); parallel tool calls; human approval points; checkpointing so a crash can resume; context hooks each iteration (clear old results, compact).

Always have hard caps and loop detection. Infinite “just one more try” is a production outage.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the skeleton you should be able to write in pseudocode. Interviewers will ask what stops the loop. “When it feels done” is not a stop condition.

## How it works + one small example

```
while steps < MAX and tokens < BUDGET and time < T:
  ctx = build(state)
  out = model(ctx)
  if identical_to_last_call(out): break_with_nudge_or_stop
  if out.tool:
    if forbidden(out.tool): observe(error)
    else: observe(run(out.tool))
  else:
    if finish_allowed(state): return out
    else: observe("cannot finish: tests not green")
  checkpoint(state)
```

Example: a coding agent hits the same failing test five times. Loop detection plus a nudge (“change approach or escalate”) beats another identical patch.

## Failure modes

1. **No step cap.** Runaway bill.

2. **Swallowed tool errors.** The model never sees why it failed.

3. **Finish without gates.** It declares victory with red tests.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The loop is assemble, call, act, observe, stop-check. I always have hard caps, I return tool errors as observations, I detect repeated calls, and I checkpoint each step.
## A concrete walk-through

MAX steps, token budget, wall clock. Identical calls nudge then stop. Finish is rejected while tests are red. Each step checkpoints. A run that swallowed tool errors is rewritten so the model sees the body. Pseudocode for this loop is what you write on the whiteboard in four minutes.

## Interview follow-up

What stops the loop? Caps, detection, gates — not “when it feels done.”

## What I would measure

Stop-reason distribution, runaway bills, and finish-with-red-tests (target zero).
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What must a robust agent loop include besides call-and-act? Stop conditions and hard budgets, error handling and retries, loop detection, checkpointing, context management each iteration, and approval points for risky actions. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is An agent repeats the same failing call forever. What do you add? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `designing-the-agent-loop`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Loop: build context, call, act, observe, check stop. Hard caps on steps, tokens, and time. Return tool errors as observations, not as silent failures. Detect identical repeated calls and nudge or stop. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `designing-the-agent-loop`.

what-the-harness-enforces.explain:
## What it is

Rules should not live only in the prompt. The harness **enforces** invariants in code: permission checks and tool allowlists; schema validation; read-before-write; refusing to mark done until tests pass; spend, time, and step limits; sandbox and path restrictions; human approval for destructive actions; redaction of secrets.

Prompts **guide**. Code **guarantees**. Use the prompt to explain why a rule exists, and code to make violations impossible or visible. Models are probabilistic; critical constraints need deterministic guards. This is also how you survive injected “ignore the rules” text.

Too many silent blocks frustrate the agent. Return a clear error that names the rule so it can adapt.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

“Never delete outside the project directory” is a code check, not a vibe. Interviewers will ask which rules you enforce versus suggest. Destructive and compliance rules go in the harness.

## How it works + one small example

`run(tool)` path: validate schema → check allowlist and path → maybe ask a human → execute in sandbox → redact → observe.

Example: finish() requires `tests_green=true` in state. The model cannot talk its way past that. Example: `rm` outside the workspace returns a structured refusal.

Write a list: guided-only (tone, style) vs enforced (money movement, deletes, PII). Review the list like an API.

## Failure modes

1. **Safety only in the prompt.** Injection or sloppiness bypasses it.

2. **Opaque blocks.** The agent retries blindly.

3. **Enforcing style.** You over-constrain harmless choices.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Prompts guide; the harness guarantees. I enforce permissions, validation, limits, and done-gates in code, and I return clear errors when I block.
## A concrete walk-through

finish() requires tests_green from a harness-run. rm outside the workspace is a structured refusal. Tone stays in the prompt. An opaque block that said “not allowed” without a reason caused retry loops; the error now names the rule and a legal path. The guided-versus-enforced list is reviewed like an API.

## Interview follow-up

Which rules are code? Destructive, money, PII, done-gates. Which are guidance? Style. Injection is why code wins.

## What I would measure

Enforced-rule bypasses, opaque-block retry loops, and approval latency for destructive tools.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: Why enforce rules in the harness and not only in the prompt? Models can ignore or be talked out of prompt rules. Code checks are deterministic, auditable, and more robust against injection. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is You want the agent to run tests before finishing. How do you enforce it? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `what-the-harness-enforces`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Prompts guide; code guarantees. Enforce permissions, schema checks, limits, and done-gates. Destructive and compliance rules do not live only in prose. Return clear errors so the agent can adapt. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `what-the-harness-enforces`.

work-across-many-context-windows.explain:
## What it is

Long-horizon tasks exceed one window. The agent works across **many context windows**, each a fresh session that must pick up where the last left off. Memory then lives in **artifacts**, not in the model’s head: progress file, decisions, next steps, a clean git state.

Pattern: an initial session sets up the environment, plan, and task list. Later sessions each do one increment, verify, commit, and update the handoff. At the start of a window, a bootstrap reads those artifacts **before** acting. At the end, leave the environment clean.

Poor handoffs cause rework and undo. Half-finished edits with no commit are how the next session guesses wrong.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the capstone idea of the level. Interviewers will ask how you finish a week-long migration with an 8k or 128k model. Sessions + artifacts is the answer.

## How it works + one small example

Session N boot: read `PROGRESS.md`, `git log -5`, failing tests. Do step 3. Run tests. Commit `step-3-handler`. Update progress. Stop.

Session N+1 does not re-plan the whole project. It reads the file.

The initial session is allowed to be broader: repo map, feature list, first failing tests. It still writes artifacts; it does not rely on its own context surviving.

## Failure modes

1. **No boot read.** The new session invents a plan.

2. **Dirty tree, no commit.** The next session cannot tell what is intentional.

3. **Handoff in chat only.** Chat is gone.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I split long work into sessions. Each one reads durable state, finishes a verified increment, commits, and writes a handoff. Memory lives in artifacts, not in the window.
## A concrete walk-through

Session 1 writes the plan and first failing tests. Session 2 reads PROGRESS.md and git log, implements the handler, commits, updates next. Session 3 does not re-plan. A session that left a dirty tree without a commit is treated as a failed handoff in the retro.

## Interview follow-up

Week-long migration on a finite window: sessions plus artifacts. Chat as memory fails.

## What I would measure

Rework rate across sessions, dirty-tree handoffs, and boots that invent a new plan.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: How can an agent finish a task far larger than its context window? Work in sessions: each reads a progress file and repository state, completes a verified increment, commits, and updates handoff notes. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is A new session redoes work already done. What is missing? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `work-across-many-context-windows`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Each window starts by reading durable state. Each window ends with a clean, written handoff. An initial session plans; later ones increment. Memory lives in artifacts, not in the model context. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `work-across-many-context-windows`.

durable-artifacts-as-the-source-of-truth.explain:
## What it is

Treat **durable artifacts** as the truth: version-controlled code and commits, a feature list with pass/fail, a progress log, test results, config. The model’s context is a temporary view of them.

Artifacts are exact, inspectable, shareable between sessions and sub-agents, and reversible. Git history is an audit trail. Prefer structured, machine-checkable formats (JSON feature list with a `passes` flag) so the agent edits a status field rather than rewriting a novel.

Protect specs and tests from self-serving edits. The agent may update **status** after verification; it may not weaken the test to make the status green without approval.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you keep a long agent honest. Interviewers will ask what happens if the model “remembers” tests passing. You re-read the artefact; you do not trust memory.

## How it works + one small example

`features.json`: `{id, spec, passes}`. The agent implements `feat-12`, runs the named test, and only then sets `passes=true`. Spec text is read-only to the agent.

Never trust “I already ran the tests” in chat. The harness runs them and writes the result.

Commits are the other artefact: one verified step, one commit, a message a later session can parse.

## Failure modes

1. **Truth in the prompt.** It will drift.

2. **Agent-editable tests.** It will game them.

3. **Prose-only feature lists.** Status cannot be checked by code.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Artifacts are the source of truth; context is a view. I use structured, checkable files, I commit after each verified step, and I protect specs and tests from the agent.
## A concrete walk-through

features.json has spec (read-only) and passes (harness-set). The model claims tests passed; the harness believes the junit artefact. A commit per verified step names the feature id. A session whose prompt said step 4 was done but git lacked the commit follows git after re-read.

## Interview follow-up

What if the model remembers tests passing? Re-read the artefact. Protect the oracle.

## What I would measure

Status/test mismatches, agent edits to protected specs, and commits without a verification artefact.
## How you would debug it on Monday

## Shipping checklist

Re-read artifacts; do not trust remembered state. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. self-run-feedback-loops.explain:
## What it is

Give the agent ways to **check its own work** and act on the result: tests, linters, type checks, builds, running the app, a screenshot or browser pass, a comparison to a spec. Without feedback the model guesses success. With deterministic signals it can detect and fix errors itself — usually a larger reliability jump than another paragraph of prompt.

Design: fast, clear, machine-readable results; compact errors (first failure plus excerpt); a rule that work is not complete until checks pass; end-to-end checks that mirror real user behaviour, not only unit stubs.

Risks: flaky tests cause thrashing; verbose logs bloat context (compact them); the agent may game the checks, so keep the check definitions out of its edit scope.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is why coding agents work at all. Interviewers ask for the strongest feedback loop on a web feature. “Run the app and the e2e checks” beats “the model is confident”.

## How it works + one small example

Loop: edit → `make test` → compact failures → edit. Finish is blocked until green. For UI, add a browser tool that asserts a selector exists.

Example: 50k of test output is reduced to the first two failures and a store id for the log. The agent does not “get lost” in stdout.

Flakes: quarantine or retry in the harness, do not let the agent rewrite the test to silence a flake.

## Failure modes

1. **No execution.** The agent is a writer, not a worker.

2. **Uncompacted logs.** The window dies.

3. **Editable oracles.** The agent lowers the bar.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I give the agent tests, linters, builds, and e2e checks it can run, I compact the feedback, and I refuse done until those checks pass. The checks are not its to weaken.
## A concrete walk-through

Edit, make test, compact first two failures, edit. Browser check asserts a selector. 50k stdout never enters the window. A flake is retried in the harness; the agent is not allowed to delete the test. Done stays blocked until the harness records green.

## Interview follow-up

Strongest loop for a web feature: run the app and e2e. Confidence is not evidence.

## What I would measure

Iterations to green, flake-induced thrashes, and done-with-red (target zero).
## How you would debug it on Monday

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: Provide tests, linters, builds, and browser or e2e checks. Completion requires passing checks recorded by the harness. Compact feedback to the first failures plus a log handle. Keep check definitions out of the agent’s edit scope. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. an-environment-agents-can-read.explain:
## What it is

Make the **environment legible** to the agent: clear repo structure, a short instruction file (AGENTS.md or similar) with commands and conventions, descriptive names, scripts for setup/test/run, structured logs, tools that expose state in readable form.

An agent has no tacit knowledge. If “how we run tests” lives in someone’s head, it will guess and burn the budget exploring. A new engineer handed only the repo is a good test: if they cannot proceed, neither can the agent.

Keep docs current. Stale command docs mislead worse than none. Prefer one-command scripts the docs point at, so the command cannot drift from the text as easily.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is cheap reliability. Interviewers will ask why an agent wasted 15 steps finding `pytest`. The answer is an agent-facing guide and a script.

## How it works + one small example

`AGENTS.md`:

```
setup: make bootstrap
test: make test
run: make dev
layout: src/ app, tests/ mirror
do not: commit secrets, edit golden files
```

Init reads this file first. Errors from `make test` should say what failed, not a stack of unrelated warnings.

Generate or test the docs: a CI step that runs the documented commands.

## Failure modes

1. **Folklore only.** The agent explores the repo blindly.

2. **Stale docs.** It runs the wrong command forever.

3. **A 40-page handbook.** It will not be read; keep a short file.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I make the repo readable: a short agent file with setup, test, and conventions, one-command scripts, and errors that say what to do. If a new engineer cannot start from the repo, the agent cannot either.
## A concrete walk-through

AGENTS.md is twelve lines: make bootstrap, make test, layout, do-nots. Boot reads it first. CI runs those make targets so the doc cannot rot. A 40-page handbook is demoted. An agent that spent 15 steps finding pytest stops doing that on this repo.

Why the wasted exploration? Folklore. New-engineer test: if they cannot start, neither can the agent.

sub-agents-for-isolated-context.explain:
## What it is

A **sub-agent** is a separate invocation with its **own fresh context**, given a focused task. It does exploratory or noisy work and returns a **condensed result** to the parent. The parent window is not polluted by thousands of tokens of search and dead ends. Sub-agents can run in parallel and can have specialised tools and instructions.

The brief must be **self-contained**; the child cannot see the parent’s prompt. Define the return format and size, limit tools and budget, and verify results before trusting them.

Costs: more total tokens, coordination, information loss in the summary. Use for broad search or independent subtasks, not tightly coupled edits to the same file.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you keep a parent planner clean. Interviewers will ask when not to use sub-agents (coupled edits, vague briefs) as well as when to use them.

## How it works + one small example

Parent: “Find where auth tokens are refreshed.” Child: repo search tools only, 8-step cap, must return `{paths[], claim, evidence_lines}`. Parent integrates and edits.

Bad: two children editing `cart.py` at once. Good: one child searches, one child reads docs, parent edits.

Verify: if the child cites a path, the parent (or harness) checks the path exists before acting.

## Failure modes

1. **Vague brief.** Garbage condensed result.

2. **Parallel writes to one file.** Conflicts.

3. **Trusting unverified claims.** The child hallucinated a path.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I use sub-agents for noisy or parallel work in a fresh window and I take back only a condensed, specified result. Briefs are self-contained, and I verify before I trust them.
## A concrete walk-through

Parent asks where tokens refresh. Child has search+read, 8 steps, must return paths, claim, quotes. Parent stats the paths before editing. Two children on cart.py at once is forbidden. A vague brief that returned a blog-post is retried with a schema. Child traces stay out of the parent window.

## Interview follow-up

When not to: coupled edits, vague briefs. When yes: noisy search, parallel read-only work. Verify claims.

## What I would measure

Parent tokens with versus without children, invalid child paths, and parallel-write conflicts.

context-budget-in-the-harness.explain:
## What it is

Give the harness an **explicit token budget** and a **policy for compact, offload, or stop**. The budget is not a comment in a prompt. It is a number the loop reads (from config or the per-turn report) and a function that chooses an action before the next call.

This ties Level 6’s accounting to the capstone: the same overflow policy you wrote for a single call now lives in the long-horizon loop. Compact elastic blocks, offload payloads, or stop and hand off. Do not enter the next model call already over the line.

The budget should include reserved output. “We still have 2k of input room” is a lie if `max_tokens` is 8k.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A long-horizon agent without a budget will eventually degrade and you will call it a model issue. Interviewers want the integer and the three actions.

## How it works + one small example

```
BUDGET = 80% of window after output reserve
if remaining < 0: stop_and_handoff
elif remaining < 10k: offload_tool_results()
elif remaining < 20k: compact_history()
```

Log the action on the turn report. Test with a fixture that would overflow a naive loop.

Tune thresholds on real traces so you compact before quality falls, not after.

## Failure modes

1. **Budget in the prompt only.** The model will “try to be concise” and still overflow.

2. **No stop.** Endless compact-and-continue on a hopeless task.

3. **Ignoring output reserve.** Provider rejects the call.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The harness has a token budget and a compact / offload / stop policy it applies before the next call. I reserve output, I log the action, and I do not leave that policy to the model.
## A concrete walk-through

The loop reads remaining after output reserve. Below 20k it compacts history; below 10k it offloads tools; at zero it stops and hands off. A prompt that said “be concise” still overflowed; the number in the loop did not. Thresholds are tuned so compact happens before the quality cliff you measured.

## Interview follow-up

Integer plus three actions, applied before the next call. Budget-in-prompt-only is the fail.

## What I would measure

Action histogram, calls sent already over budget (target zero), and quality versus remain-room.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What does a context budget in the harness include besides a number? A policy that chooses compact, offload, or stop, applied before the next call, with output reserved in the remaining-room math. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is Why not put the budget only in the system prompt? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `context-budget-in-the-harness`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: The harness holds an explicit token budget, not a prompt hint. Policy actions: compact, offload, or stop. Apply the policy before the next model call. Reserve output when you compute remaining room. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `context-budget-in-the-harness`.

progress-file-as-the-window.explain:
## What it is

Treat the **progress file as what survives a window reset**, not the chat transcript. After a crash, a cap, or a new session, the transcript may be gone or untrustworthy. The progress file (plus git and tests) is the window you actually have.

That means the file must be complete enough to restart: goal, status of steps, next action, blockers, pointers to notes and result ids. If a fact matters and is not in an artefact, it does not survive.

Write the file **during** the run, not as a last polite gesture that a killed process will skip. The harness can write it even when the model forgets.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the operational slogan of long-horizon work. Interviewers will ask what you reload after a 128k window is exhausted. “The transcript” is the wrong answer.

## How it works + one small example

On every status change, the harness updates `PROGRESS.md` (or JSON) itself, using the model’s proposed edit only after validation. On boot, the assembler reads that file into a pinned block and **does not** require the old chat.

Example: process killed at step 6. New window: goal still there, steps 1–5 done with commit SHAs, step 6 doing, next = rerun test X. No archaeology in logs required.

If the model writes a beautiful recap only in chat, copy the must-keep lines into the file in the same step.

## Failure modes

1. **File as optional diary.** It lags the truth.

2. **Trusting the old transcript on reset.** It may be truncated or from another task.

3. **Missing pointers.** Notes exist but the new session cannot find them.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The progress file is the window that survives a reset. I keep it complete and harness-written, and I boot from it instead of from the old chat.
## A concrete walk-through

Kill the process at step 6. The new window boots from PROGRESS.md: goal, 1–5 with SHAs, 6 doing, next = rerun test X. Old chat is not loaded. A diary that lagged one step behind caused a redo; the harness now writes on status change, including when the model forgets.

## Interview follow-up

What do you reload after the window is exhausted? The file, git, tests — not the transcript.

## What I would measure

Cold-boot success without chat, file-lag incidents, and missing pointers to notes.
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What should survive a window reset, and what should not be trusted? The progress file, git state, and test artefacts survive. The old chat transcript should not be required or blindly trusted. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is The process dies mid-step and the progress file still says step 5 todo. What failed? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `progress-file-as-the-window`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: The progress file, not the transcript, survives a window reset. It must contain goal, statuses, next action, and pointers. The harness writes it on every status change. Boot reads the file into a pinned block. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `progress-file-as-the-window`.

isolated-sub-agent-contracts.explain:
## What it is

An **isolated sub-agent contract** specifies **what the child may see** and **what it must return** so the parent window stays small. Isolation is not automatic just because you opened another socket. If you paste the parent’s entire transcript into the child, you have two large windows and no win.

The contract has an **input allowlist** (brief, needed files, allowed tools, budget) and an **output schema** (size cap, required fields, evidence). The harness enforces both: it builds the child prompt from the allowlist only, and it rejects or truncates returns that do not match.

This is how sub-agents stay an isolation tool rather than a fork-bomb of context.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask how you stop a child from bloating the parent. A contract with a size cap and a schema is the answer. “We tell it to be concise” is not.

## How it works + one small example

```
input: {goal, constraints[], paths[], tools: [search, read], max_steps: 8}
output: {claim, paths[], quotes[] }  # max 800 tokens
```

Parent is not in `input`. Child traces are not appended to the parent — only the validated `output`.

If the child returns 6k of rambling, the harness keeps the schema fields and stores the rest under an id, or rejects and retries with a tighter reminder.

## Failure modes

1. **Pasting the parent transcript into the child.** Isolation is gone.

2. **Unvalidated returns.** The parent is stuffed again.

3. **No tool allowlist.** The child has the same blast radius as the parent.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I specify what a sub-agent may see and what it must return. The harness builds the child prompt from that allowlist and accepts only a small, valid result back into the parent.
## A concrete walk-through

Input allowlist is goal, three paths, search+read, eight steps. Output is claim+paths+quotes, 800 tokens. Parent history is not in the child. A 6k rant is schema-sliced and the rest stored. Off-contract tools are rejected. Isolation is measured: child prompt size versus parent, not “we opened another call.”

## Interview follow-up

How do you stop the child from bloating the parent? Contract, allowlist, size cap. Pasting the parent transcript voids isolation.

## What I would measure

Child prompt size, rejected returns, and accidental parent-transcript pastes (target zero).
## How you would debug it on Monday

Pick one failing request and open the rendered prompt, not the template. The first question to answer is the one you already drill in review: What does an isolated sub-agent contract specify? The input allowlist the child may see and the output schema and size it must return, so the parent window stays small. If the per-block token map disagrees with the model's story, believe the map. The second pass is A parent pastes its full history into every child ‘for context’. What did you lose? against the same dump. Most leaks that look like a model regression are an assembler, cap, or harness miss on `isolated-sub-agent-contracts`.

## Shipping checklist

Treat these as gates, not slogans: A contract names what the child may see and what it must return. The harness builds the child prompt from an input allowlist only. Returns are schema-checked and size-capped before they enter the parent. Do not paste the parent transcript into the child. If you cannot show a trace that proves each gate, this practice is not shipped. Add one eval or fixture that fails when the practice is skipped, and keep the apply, debug, recall questions in the review set so a new teammate can rehearse the same fork. Re-run that fixture when the model, the assembler, or the tool menu changes — those are the edits that quietly undo `isolated-sub-agent-contracts`.
